Oral evidence - 18 Nov 2026

Energy Security and Net Zero Committee

Oral evidence: Preparing for winter, HC 749

Wednesday 18 November 2026

Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 18 November 2026.

Watch the meeting

Members present: Bill Esterson (Chair); Torcuil Crichton; Graeme Downie; Wera Hobhouse; Melanie Onn; Mike Reader; Claire Young.

Questions 1 - 124

Witnesses

I: Nye Jones, Head of Campaigns, Generation Rent; Alex Belsham-Harris, Head of Energy Consumer Markets, Citizens Advice; Dr Katie Barrett, ECO4 Justice Campaigner, Fuel Poverty Action.

II: Neil Kenward, Director General for Markets, Ofgem; Ed Dodman, Chief Executive Officer and Chief Ombudsman, Energy Ombudsman.

III: Martin McCluskey MP, Minister for Local Energy and Jobs, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero; David Thomas, Interim Director General, Household Consumers and Energy Retail, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero; Ben Golding, Director of Affordability and Retail, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Nye Jones, Alex Belsham-Harris and Dr Katie Barrett.

Chair: Welcome to this morning’s session of the Energy Security and Net Zero Select Committee. This is our session on preparing for winter, on a day when Cornwall Insight is predicting that the price cap could rise by 26%, which is a significant increase on its previous estimate. It is a very timely session for the Committee and, more importantly, for those people who face the challenge of rising energy bills. I will ask our first panel to introduce themselves and then we will go into the questioning.

Dr Barrett: I am a scientist. I am a victim of the ECO4 scheme and am here as a member of Fuel Poverty Action. I am part of a group of hundreds of victims representing the thousands of victims of ECO4. I am also, when I am not doing that, on the advisory committee for Indoor Air Aware on mould remediation and the health impacts of mould, because I am a biological scientist, not a medical doctor.

We estimate that there are over 100,000 houses that have been damaged by the ECO4 thing. As far as I am aware, none of them has been properly remediated, and certainly none in our group has. I know that some people have been sent to the National Energy Foundation but no work has been released. Nothing has been greenlit—nothing—and that is months and months after having met with Martin McCluskey in June and explaining the scale of the problem to him.

There are also a huge number of issues with people trying to navigate a system that is very broken. At Fuel Poverty Action we campaign on energy injustice. There is a massive problem in terms of energy bills, as you already highlighted, Mr Esterson, but particularly for people who have had installation that has been done badly. There are people who have heat pumps that do not work and do not heat their houses because the insulation was done so poorly that the heat loss is too much to allow heat pumps. People are having to revert to putting gas boilers in to heat their home above 13 degrees.

There is a very serious problem. There are a lot of households being affected by it, and they are vulnerable people. They are people who were eligible for a scheme that was there for vulnerable people. There are loads of us suffering and it is heartbreaking.

Chair: Katie, thank you very much for your comments. We will come back to some of that, including being able to put some of your points to the Minister a little later on today. We very much appreciate what you have just been saying. We will ask Alex and Nye to introduce themselves first and then go on to some other questions.

Alex Belsham-Harris: I am Alex Belsham-Harris. I am head of energy consumer markets at Citizens Advice.

Nye Jones: Hi. I am Nye Jones. I am head of campaigns at Generation Rent. We campaign for private renters across the UK.

Chair: You are all very welcome. I mentioned the increase in the price cap that is predicted by Cornwall Insight. What does the increase in cost mean for families, quite apart from what Katie was saying there? Perhaps Alex and Nye can address that.

Alex Belsham-Harris: As you say, we are seeing prices returning to the levels that they were back in the depths of the 2022-23 energy crisis with the kinds of predictions we are seeing today. As you say, it is a 20%-plus increase. Because this is taking place in the coldest months of the year, we anticipate that it will mean people paying around £200 more on energy between January and March next year compared with what they were paying a year ago.

We know that this comes at a time when, for many households, budgets are already not in a good place. At Citizens Advice, just thinking about the people who come to us with debt, we are now supporting people with an average debt of over £10,000 and an average energy debt of over £2,000. Even after we have helped them with their debts and looked to see whether there are other things they can do to maximise their income—benefits and those sorts of things—over half of those households still do not have enough money to cover their essentials. It is coming at a very damaging time for households.

We know that the Government have responded with a support scheme—the £100 rebate for people living in properties in bands A to D. That will be a helpful measure for some people—people who are not facing the highest bill rises or are not on the lowest incomes—but we are concerned that, for people who are struggling most, that will not be anywhere near enough to mitigate the impact that they are seeing.

Chair: Before I move on to Nye, what is your view of the Ofgem debt relief scheme? How effective is it going to be?

Alex Belsham-Harris: It is really positive that at the Budget the Government announced that the debt relief scheme will go ahead. It has been in development for quite a while and significantly delayed, so we want to see it brought forward as quickly as possible.

We are expecting a consultation on the details, but our concerns about the effectiveness of the scheme at this point probably relate to the eligibility period. The debts that are eligible are from 2022 to 2024, and lots of people will have continued to build up significant debts from that point onwards, which will not be within the scope of the scheme.

The benefit of the scheme should be to re-engage people, help them set up a repayment plan and find the best way to pay for them and what other support there is, but those benefits of engagement will be much lower to consumers if they think, “This scheme will wipe off only 20% or 30% of the debt that I owe” because it has grown so much. We need to see the detail about how that engagement will be maximised to ensure that as many people as possible can benefit from that scheme once it is in place.

I should say that there is one other positive. The other change that was made was a slight broadening of eligibility so that it is not just households on means-tested benefits, but pensioners and people with disabilities. Those changes are positive, but we have a lot of concerns as well.

Chair: You would like to see a higher figure for debt write-off, which is something we proposed, as you will realise, in a previous inquiry.

Alex Belsham-Harris: We need to see what other measures could go alongside. If there is no scope to change the period in which the debts are covered, we would want to see what other measures can go in alongside, whether that is action by energy suppliers to top up whatever the write-off is, or other measures that can mean that people see this as a really positive offer that is worth engaging with. Otherwise we do not think that it will be as successful as it could be.

Chair: Nye, do you have anything to add to what Alex has said on those topics?

Nye Jones: For private renters specifically, the vicious combination of unaffordable rents, soaring energy bills and the fact that we tend to live in very cold, draughty homes means that this coming winter will probably be the most difficult in recent history. To put that into a bit of perspective, renters on average spend 36% of our income on rent, but in major cities that jumps to well over 40%. Compare that with owner-occupiers with a mortgage, for whom the average is 19%. At the same time, 49% of rented homes in England are below EPC C, compared with just around 25% of social homes. Renters are being hit with really high rents that take up too much of our income and living in cold homes with really high energy bills.

With the recent price cap increase, Ofgem estimated the annual household fuel bill increase would be £60, but our modelling found that, for a family living in an EPC D, it will actually be around £180, and in an EPC E, which is the current minimum standard in private renting, it jumps to over £200 a year. This is huge pressure coming from lots of different sides. I agree with Alex that we are looking at going back towards the debts of 2022. I would argue that it is possibly even worse, given that Ofgem decreased the typical domestic consumption values in July that make up the predicted price cap.

With that being said, we were pleased to see the Government recognise that more universal support is needed, beyond the warm home discount, in the autumn Budget. We feel like the £100 rebate was poorly targeted. Council tax bands were set in 1991 and there will be a lot of private renters who should receive it who will not, particularly those in house shares in cities, where the value of the home is not consistent with the salaries of the people within it. While it was good to see the expansion of the warm home discount recently, the level of rebate people receive through that is not keeping up with rising bills: people received £140 in 2021; it is now £150, but annual energy bills are set to rise by around £1,000 a year. Unfortunately, we need to see higher Government support this winter.

Chair: How would you target Government support to be more effective?

Nye Jones: There is a range of ways. At the moment, with the warm home discount, there are a lot of private renters on lower incomes who are paying far more of their income than they should on rent who will not receive it. Expanding it, and looking particularly at homes with an EPC below C, would be a really good start. There are particular regionalities. For example, in some areas of Birmingham 80% of private rented homes are below C, compared with parts of London where 80% are above C.

The HMO register could be looked at as well. As I said, people in house shares and large living situations in the main will not receive the £100 rebate. There is a need to understand the whole picture, rather than just looking at someone’s income. For example, an owner-occupier who has no mortgage but is on a low income will be in a much better place than a private renter in work who is spending 45% or 50% of their income on rent. I feel like the council tax bands are a slightly lazy way of targeting support.

Chair: I am not sure I have heard you give an alternative, which perhaps explains the challenge for the Government in designing a plan.

Nye Jones: It is a challenge, but it is one that could be overcome with Government resources.

Dr Barrett: Some £6 billion has been added to our bills to fund the ECO4 thing and I am pretty sure the savings are not actually happening, given the reports of people’s bills going up by three times because of botched insulation meaning that air-source heat pumps do not work, for example. It was the energy company obligation, but it has resulted in £6 billion going on to the bills of the public as a whole. That is not going to be helping the rates that people are paying either. Energy is insanely expensive, to the point that people cannot afford to put their heating on.

Mike Reader: Alex, the Government have had a focus on warm homes, and rightly so. Since the election, have things got better for those people who were struggling to heat their homes?

Alex Belsham-Harris: Based on the client data and the people we are supporting at Citizens Advice, in many areas that is not the case. There are changes that are in development, and that we want to see delivered soon, that could help people, so I do not want to be overly negative. For example, there was the change to expand the warm home discount scheme to more households, which meant more people were getting that support. Unfortunately, because that is funded through bills, it also meant that the net benefit of the support reduced for everyone who received it, and particularly for those who had been in receipt of it before. That sort of change has a mixture of winners and losers.

We have seen the positive action to take some of the levy costs off bills, which has brought electricity costs down for some households, in particular those that use traditional electric storage heaters. We know that that was a helpful step, but a lot of these measures have been completely swallowed up by the massive increase in wholesale gas costs that we have seen following the conflict in Iran. Although they are there and having that impact on people’s bills, which would be even higher without those measures, we are in a crisis situation.

Looking to the future at what further changes might come through that would help people, we definitely support the changes in the Energy Independence Bill that will put in place a better legislative framework for delivering targeted support. We need much clearer sense of what is being done on the data matching side to deliver that in practice.

Mike Reader: Have the Government been slow off the mark on this?

Alex Belsham-Harris: Data matching—deciding what data we can use to support people through schemes such as the warm home discount that currently exists—has been a known issue since the last crisis, when we had to introduce support for absolutely everyone in the country to prevent bills from going up. Successive Governments have said that this is something that they are looking at and working on. We have seen very little progress in terms of what is known publicly about the capability around data matching. That, I think, is part of the reason why we have ended up having to use council tax bands as a way of targeting support this winter.

Mike Reader: Nye, what about for renters? Have things got better since the election?

Nye Jones: Yes and no. We saw the passing and implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act in May. That has been a major change that has redressed the power imbalance somewhat between tenants and landlords, and we celebrated that. If we think of the cost of homes and the foundations of existence, such as energy, things have almost certainly got worse. When you look at it in the round, that combination of high rents, which in our view the Renters’ Rights Act does not solve, lack of supply of homes—you will have seen multiple news reports about this being delayed—and soaring bills means that renters will be feeling significantly worse off.

There is the continued freeze of local housing allowance, for example. Rents have risen by 23% since it was last uplifted. Nearly 60% of renters who receive housing benefit or the housing element of universal credit have a shortfall between their rent and what they receive. That pulls them into fuel poverty when you bring everything in the round. I would say that renters feel more secure, but probably have less money in their back pocket.

Mike Reader: Is money the only answer? We have talked about needing more support for debt relief, incentives and support for households. Are there other ways that we can alleviate the problems, rather than spending more money on the issue?

Nye Jones: The Government’s raising of the minimum energy efficiency standard for private rented homes is really positive. From 2030, all private rented homes, unless they have certain exemptions, will need to be at EPC C, up from EPC E. This is a much better longer-term solution to reduce fuel poverty among renters and make homes cheaper to heat. As I heard the Minister say previously, the cheapest energy is the energy you do not use. That is positive.

We were slightly disappointed that some of that was watered down a little. The cost cap that sets the maximum that a landlord can spend was reduced from £15,000 to £10,000. We also saw the timeline put back. Originally it was 2028 for new tenancies, but now it is 2030 without question. We are also concerned in that regard about the prospect of landlords hiking the rent after investing to retrofit homes and tenants having little power to prevent that. In terms of the long term, that is where we would see addressing the key issue of fuel poverty among private renters, and obviously uplifting LHA as well.

In the short term, we have been supportive of a social tariff to potentially replace the warm home discount. We are pleased to see the Government giving themselves the power to bring that in through the Energy Independence Bill. We think that would allow for that wider targeting piece that I talked about at the start, and staggered discounts. There are a lot of people who are not in the traditional targeted benefits world who will be really struggling now.

Mike Reader: Alex, are there other ways to alleviate the problem rather than more money?

Alex Belsham-Harris: It is a good challenge. There are other ways of making better use of the existing money that is going into the system. That is why we are very passionate about this point around data matching. If you have better data and targeting, you can make the money that you are already spending go further by reaching the people where it will have the most impact.

There are also decisions about where the money that funds the energy system is recovered from—not necessarily changing the amount of money that is recovered, but whether it is recovered from bill payers or taxpayers or different groups of bill payers. That comes with some risks. On the gas standing charge side, for example, we have concerns that there will be winners from that change who will see benefits, but also people who will lose out. There are challenges when you are moving money between groups of consumers like that.

More widely, there are also benefits through smart technology and smart metering that mean that the support suppliers can provide is in a better place than it used to be. There are other things that are not purely fiscal.

Dr Barrett: I am really concerned that the Government are moving on from the ECO4 thing, which is a massive problem that has pushed people into worse fuel poverty. There are stories from lots of victims about being passed from one person to another. I can give you an example from this week. I had an email from Ofgem saying, “We can’t tell you if the measures have been removed. You have to speak to DESNZ.” That was after I had had an email from DESNZ telling me, “No, Ofgem is looking into that.” I am trying to think of a polite analogy, but it is not joined up and there is no accountability.

So much money has been wasted and that is making everything more expensive for everybody—not just the victims of the ECO4 scandal, but every single person who is paying for energy and paying ridiculously high energy bills. I know that there are external factors in that as well, but there are lots of things that could be done to mitigate that.

I worry that the new scheme is just going to be throwing more money away. They have not resolved anything with ECO4. That is still ongoing. The scale of the warm home scheme is three times the amount and they do not have the people to actually do it. There are not skilled people doing it. Everything has been done in a really non-evidence-based way. There is no proper quantification of any of the measures that is being done properly. Nothing is being done properly, which means that people are left with wet, mouldy homes that they cannot heat. It is pushing them further and further into fuel poverty.

Chair: Katie, I should say that we will put your questions—and, indeed, the points made by the other panellists—to both Ofgem and the Minister. This is super helpful.

Claire Young: Today is Fuel Poverty Awareness Day. Do you believe that the Government have a strategy to address fuel poverty in the long term, or do you think they are simply applying a sticking plaster each winter?

Dr Barrett: Absolutely a sticking plaster, and one that is falling off. It is a sticking plaster that is being stuck on to wet walls and just falling straight off again. The ECO4 scheme has been an absolute scandal.

I have a question; it is not directly relevant to what you have just asked me, but it is tangential. For the company that did my installation, I have so much evidence of fraud. I have photographs of things that never existed that it said were there. I have photographs that have dates on them that are literally impossible. I presented all that to Ofgem months ago and have not had any kind of response back. The Serious Fraud Office is not doing anything.

This company has gone into liquidation. It has limited liability—I appreciate that—but it has committed crime, so surely the director of that company should be held to account for the criminal acts that he and his company did. I am talking about false names on paperwork, fraudulent signatures and lots of falsified data. I know that this is not unique to that company. There is a lot of phoenixing going on. There is a major issue of accountability. These companies go into liquidation and then TrustMark says, “They are not part of our scheme any more, so we cannot help you.” There are people literally going out of their minds trying to get this stuff sorted. Yes, it is a sticking plaster.

There is this whole thing with plug-in solar. I do not think that any scientists, architects or engineers were consulted about whether that was a good idea, because that is clearly set up to fail. It is a very easy, performative thing to say, “Look, we have an idea.” It is yet another one.

Installing air-source heat pumps into properties that have not been properly insulated is not going to work. It is proven by the epic failings of the ECO4 scheme. It is not going to work. We know that it does not work. There was even a paper written on it by somebody called Kirk Archibald in 2022. I have the reference for it somewhere. He wrote about the problems with trying to apply retrofit if people are not skilled enough to do it properly.

It is a sticking plaster. In my house, they put insulation over wet, mouldy walls. I queried it and they said, “It is fine. It will not come through.” I said, “Hang on, mould likes dark, wet places. That is a very bad idea.” This was February 2024.

Claire Young: We will definitely be putting those points to Ofgem and the Minister later.

Dr Barrett: They are not quantifying the fixes either. They are not being transparent about the numbers. There are so many properties that have been damaged and people are still trying to get remediation. As far as I can tell, nobody has had any work remediated. People are facing their third or fourth freezing cold winter in houses that are not safe and are absolutely riddled with mould.

It is heartbreaking hearing some of the stories. I was talking to a friend yesterday who is one of the other campaigners. She also came to meet Martin McCluskey in June. She was one of the few people where the company doing her remediation had not gone into liquidation, and it has just gone into liquidation. She has only got half the radiators up in her house, and her house was 13 degrees and freezing cold. It is horrific.

Claire Young: Absolutely. We will definitely be putting those points later.

Alex Belsham-Harris: What has happened to Katie and the other people whose cases she has described is obviously horrendous and reflects similar cases that we have seen at Citizens Advice, where people have had poor experiences of energy-efficiency installation. A really top priority for us is fixing the consumer protection framework around energy efficiency. That is something that the Government need to prioritise in their strategy around fuel poverty and energy affordability more generally

Some steps are being taken, including a consultation on the new consumer protection framework, which has some really positive elements, replacing some of the patchwork of protections that currently exist and giving much clearer access to redress and much clearer and stronger enforcement. We need to see that come in quite quickly if it is going to be aligned with the delivery of the next element of the warm homes plan for low-income households, because we cannot risk these sorts of issues arising again in future.

On your broader point around whether there is a strategy on fuel poverty, the Government have taken steps that have addressed energy affordability, but they have not always thought about or fully considered the impacts on some fuel-poor households. For example, as I said, expanding the warm home discount earlier in the Parliament helped those households that received that. The ones that then had to pay towards the cost of that scheme and saw a lower net benefit were households that had higher energy usage in general and were more likely to be in fuel poverty. They now get less net support from that scheme than they did.

Similarly, as we implement the decision on gas standing charges, there is a risk for people who have the highest energy usage. I think there are estimates that around 5% to 10% of households on low incomes will see their bills rise by about £50 when gas standing charges have moved into unit rates. Those will be the households that already have the highest bills and are most likely to be in fuel poverty. It is vital that, as part of any fuel poverty strategy, we are offsetting those risks and going further.

Claire Young: Do you have any proposals for how to do that?

Alex Belsham-Harris: It comes back to data matching: understanding how we can identify which those households are, what data is available, who we want to target and which households the Government are most worried about in terms of their losing out. We are particularly concerned that it will be families with children and households where people are disabled that are going to see the biggest increases. Resolution Foundation analysis showed that only 30% of households with three or more children will see lower bills as a result of the gas standing charge changes.

There is data available around people who receive benefits linked to having children or disability that could be used to target support. There are other options around income data that I think the Government have been developing plans for. We do not have a transparent sense of what is feasible in the timeline allowed. We have about a year until the Government have said they want to implement this change to gas standing charges. That is a very short timeframe to develop a system that mitigates for everyone we might be concerned about losing out. We may end up in a situation where there is a very minimum level of mitigation unless the timeline is extended.

Nye Jones: The question was whether the Government have a strategy. In terms of private renters, it is a mixed bag. As I said previously, we were really pleased to see the ambition of the new minimum energy efficiency standard of private rented homes being put into law. The previous Government talked about doing this and then backtracked. We have seen that landlords will not make those investments unless they are forced to. That is a positive and in the long term we hope that that will raise close to 500,000 households out of fuel poverty.

The issues come in the shorter term and in the way support while that process happens is targeted. A lot of it comes down to the way we measure fuel poverty. In England, if you live in an EPC C or above you cannot be categorised as in fuel poverty. As a renter, you could be spending half of your income on rent, while your bills are still soaring and you are struggling to put the heating on, even if you are living in a home that is at the new minimum standard. More broadly, it is about understanding that soaring bills and rent are pulling more people into this mix than has previously been recognised.

I was talking to a renter the other day who is in her early 60s but in work, so she does not receive the warm home discount. She is facing a 6% rent increase. That will mean her rent has increased by 18% in the past three years. She lives in an EPC D and says that she is terrified of turning on the heating this winter. She said that the £100 rebate will only go towards her rent and food. It will barely touch the sides of her bill. We are seeing that people who traditionally the Government have not thought they needed to support with bills are now going to be really struggling.

Graeme Downie: I want to pick up some of that, but to talk in particular about the technology that is used in different rented properties. Nye, a tenant in fuel poverty usually has little or no say in what technology is used in their home. It is based on whatever the landlord has installed. How much impact does the heating system itself have on whether a household ends up in fuel poverty and is there a particular group that is worse off?

Nye Jones: Yes, definitely. Any home that is electric only is far more expensive to heat. It is around 2.5 times more expensive. The big issue for rented households, though, as I said before, is the overall energy efficiency rating, particularly in terms of insulation. Homes that are D and E are far more expensive. They do not keep the heat in and become far more expensive to heat. Landlords have not made those fabric improvements to improve insulation. That is a major issue facing renters, and renters obviously do not have power to do that themselves.

Graeme Downie: Is there anything that could be done to address that and to give renters more say, influence or knowledge even of how different technologies are working prior to them being installed? Are there any requirements you could put in place?

Nye Jones: The Government are setting up the Warm Homes Agency as part of the warm homes plan. We would really like to see that have a consumer and renter-focused part to give advice to renters on this issue.

This new minimum standard will come in by 2030, but the warm homes local grant already exists, which can fund retrofit improvements where tenants are on low incomes. Many tenants do not know it exists and the Government could do a lot more to advertise it. Tenants could speak to their landlords, for example, and push them. They could apply for these grants and get those works done earlier so they are living in warmer homes now, rather than in 2030.

Graeme Downie: To your mind, would that be a requirement that would have to be included? Should a landlord be required to speak to their tenant prior to doing upgrades? What would it look like beyond just advice? We see lots of Government advice that no one knows about, either landlord or tenant, so no one knows they are meant to do it.

Nye Jones: The problem we face is that often neither landlord nor tenant is at all expert in energy. That is why it comes back down to advice. The Warm Homes Agency will play a critical role in making sure landlords take the right form of action for a home. We would see that ideally, in most cases, as a fabric-first insulation approach to make sure that the energy efficiency rating improves.

Graeme Downie: Presumably you would encourage that to be a three-way conversation between the advice, the tenant and the landlord, rather than just being landlord to landlord, kind of muddling through on their own.

Nye Jones: It is important that the tenant understands the work that is being done and why, and the potential benefit. One concern we have is that there is little to stop a landlord increasing the rent afterwards. It is estimated it would cost £6,000 to £7,000 to take a home from D, which is where about 37% of private rented homes are, to C. The tribunal where tenants can challenge rent increases considers energy efficiency when looking at the market value of a home. There is little to stop a landlord increasing the rent afterwards and the tribunal looking at any case and saying, “That is fair, because the home has gone up from D to C and will command a higher market value.” We are really keen to see some changes there, particularly around cost neutrality, to make sure that any rent increase does not go further than any potential bill savings.

Graeme Downie: So any rent increase should match the investment that is being made.

Nye Jones: We would prefer no rent increase.

Graeme Downie: Yes, of course, but at the very least it should be proportional.

Nye Jones: Yes, it should not cancel out the bill savings. This policy is about fuel poverty; it is not about bringing rents up.

Graeme Downie: Alex, picking up on what Nye said about tenants, in particular, on all-electric heating, what data does Citizens Advice have that emphasises, perhaps, or proves that point? Are they over-represented in energy debt? To what extent does that come through?

Alex Belsham-Harris: The key data we tend to look at there is the data published by the Committee on Fuel Poverty, which has a great dataset of impacts for different households, including people on electric heating. That shows that those are the households in the deepest fuel poverty, so the gap they need to fill is biggest. Other data that is available shows that those households are much more likely to live in a rented situation than other households. We tend to focus on that.

When we see cases at Citizens Advice where people have those legacy electric heating systems, they are often struggling with really significant bills because they might be old and inefficient. We know from research that people often struggle with the heating controls for those types of heating. Heating controls are an important aspect in general, in terms of understanding how your boiler works or, if you are on a heat network, how that works and how you manage it in a way that aligns best with the right tariff. These are things that people need to have a good understanding of to get the best outcome.

Graeme Downie: You have picked up on exactly the next thing I wanted to ask you. How do we start addressing that? To be honest—you mentioned it as well, Katie—someone puts in a new bit of technology and I have no idea whether that works. I have no idea whether it is working properly for a start. I am trusting someone that it has gone in and that is fine.

Dr Barrett: Nor do the people who are fitting it, because they are not qualified.

Graeme Downie: To either Katie or Alex, from a Citizens Advice perspective, whether it is a tenant, a landlord or an owner-occupier, how do we make sure that they understand in a more active way the technology that is being put in, rather than passive information being available should they choose to look?

Alex Belsham-Harris: We think that clear information from the installer is a vital part of that, and then access to independent advice about how to use these things efficiently and decide whether they are right for you in the first place. With the landlord and tenant situation there are more challenges, because the person paying for the installation and the person living with it are different. There are split responsibilities, as there are when people are moving properties.

Graeme Downie: Is that something you would expect the Warm Homes Agency to do and provide effectively? If a landlord calls up and says, “This is what I am doing. I am acting in good faith”—let us for the moment say the landlord is acting in good faith—is it then helpful if the Warm Homes Agency says, “Have you discussed this with your tenant?” to help them through a managed process? That is picking up some of the things that Nye was saying earlier on.

Alex Belsham-Harris: The Warm Homes Agency, as has been discussed, will have a major role to play in overseeing the overall consumer journey that people are going through, including people in rented housing. That will be a really important part of that. There will be a range of routes to deliver advice. We do not necessarily think that the Warm Homes Agency should be the one giving all the advice, because that may not be what best suits its role, but it should give guidance around how that should be managed.

There may be different approaches needed in the rented sector. If you are a social housing provider, it is much more likely that you will be able to do things such as welcome packs for tenants that explain the heating system across an entire development, particularly where there is a heat network. Where there is a private tenant relationship, what is needed and how to best deliver that might be slightly different. There may be a role for lettings agents, for example, in that process as well. It is something where we really want to see clear guidance developed.

Nye Jones: There is a role for local authorities as well, especially when we will see the roll-out of the new “register your rental property” database from the end of this year. That will provide much better information about homes in a local authority’s area and the EPC rating of those homes. There should be work for local authorities to do to understand the percentage of homes in their area that will need retrofit improvements by 2030 and potentially provide advice to landlords and tenants during that process.

Graeme Downie: Should part of that be helping tenants or people in fuel poverty to access flexibility within tariffs? This has come up in other evidence sessions. The concern has been raised previously that flexibility in tariffs sounds great, but it is normally accessed only by those who can, frankly, afford it and, I presume, mostly owner-occupiers. How do we make sure that that is locked in? We have heard some very good examples about social housing, but they seem to be quite isolated. How do we make sure that that is baked into what the Warm Homes Agency is doing as well? Sorry, Katie, I am aware that I have moved on a little bit. I will ask you for your comments in a second.

Alex Belsham-Harris: The prerequisite for benefiting from flexibility is having a smart meter, and we know that private renters are less likely to have smart meters. The first step we need to take is to improve the access of those groups to smart metering, because there are loads of benefits around getting away from estimated bills as well as accessing flexibility. In the debt circuit breaker that the Government and Ofgem published, there was a commitment to improving tenant access to smart meters so that landlords cannot object to those being installed. That is the first step.

We know that the people who will benefit most from flexibility will be those who have low-carbon technologies installed, which may be less likely in rented properties. Over time, that may adjust. It is about how we improve people’s access to those technologies and, once they are in their home, particularly if it is a rented home that they have moved into newly, their ability to understand what is there and how to use it most effectively and flexibly. We want to avoid what we have seen with storage heaters and Economy 7—the traditional way of doing this. We know that lots of people moved in, had no idea what their tariff was and no idea how the heating system worked effectively, and saw higher bills as a result.

Graeme Downie: Katie, is there anything there you want to pick up? We are talking a lot here about things that are happening lots of winters hence. We should be talking as well about what we can do in the shorter term. Is there anything that you would like to pick up from your own experience on what actions the Government should be taking now to make sure the things you have described do not happen again?

Dr Barrett: As I said, lots of people are going into their third or fourth winter with wet, mouldy, cold homes that they cannot heat because they have air-source heat pumps that do not work. MCS has only checked a few of them. The Government need to be holding these assurance bodies to account.

You go into the complaints process and it takes six months with each body. For mine it was NAPIT and then TrustMark. It took six months with NAPIT and then it said, “There is nothing we can do. We have removed their accreditation, so we cannot do anything now.” TrustMark did not reply for a whole year and that was its response. If you have people who are supposed to be the assurance bodies for these various technologies—MCS for air-source heat pumps, for example—but they do not actually do anything when an installer bodges it, other than removing their accreditation, and do not actually fix the problem, it is a massive waste of money.

Graeme Downie: I am aware that the next session we have is with the ombudsman and Ofgem—

Chair: We need to move on. We have had one inquiry where we have seen the scale of the problem with ECO, and we are about to do an inquiry on warm homes as well, so we will certainly be picking these points up, and not just today.

Dr Barrett: I also know that, with part L, there are not enough qualified people who know how these new technologies work. Over 50% of the construction workforce is over 50. I am over 50; I am not saying that you cannot teach an old dog new tricks, but, at the same time, people are not going to want to learn completely new technology, and they clearly do not know what they are doing.

Torcuil Crichton: Thank you all for coming in. I will pick up on what Graeme was about to talk about on the ombudsman and Ofgem. Things do go wrong—they often go wrong. We hear about it a lot as a Committee and as individual MPs. Notwithstanding what you said, Katie, about things going very wrong with installation, often the relationship between the consumer and the energy company goes wrong. We would like to know how that can be fixed. Alex, what is the commonest thing that goes wrong and what are the quickest fixes?

Alex Belsham-Harris: The most common issues that we are seeing at the moment at Citizens Advice through our consumer service helpline, which is our specialist energy service, are around energy affordability and billing. Billing is still normally, month to month, either the first or second most common issue that we are seeing. It is important to put that into some context. Those cases have fallen slightly year on year. When we look at surveys, we know that overall satisfaction with billing has been going up, but there is a range of performance between suppliers. As we go into a winter where prices are rising, if your bill has mistakes in it, the impact that could have on you in terms of cost is significant. It is an area that we need firms to continue to focus on.

Torcuil Crichton: It is an exhausting process of going to the electricity company, coming back to the electricity company, appealing it and going to the ombudsman. Could that be tightened or shortened? Could the rein be shorter?

Alex Belsham-Harris: The changes that the Government have announced—moving to a six-week wait before you can take your case to the ombudsman—we think achieve the right balance between giving consumers and energy suppliers time to address issues and being able to quickly move on to the Energy Ombudsman at that point. The Energy Ombudsman is also committed to resolving cases more quickly. All that is positive. We want to make sure that people who need more time are not feeling rushed through the processes and that, where people need other types of support, whether that is advice or support from organisations such as the extra help unit, which can intercede on behalf of people in vulnerable circumstances, they are reaching those where appropriate. Those also are really important routes for people to resolve their problems.

To finish answering your first question on what can be done around billing, the work that Ofgem is doing to introduce a billing outcome and its broader shift to outcomes-based regulation could offer real benefits if we see a much clearer focus on who the poor performers are and how we address the challenges in billing, as long as we retain and potentially strengthen the vital backstop protections, such as the back billing rule, which means you cannot be billed for energy used more than a year ago. There is work under way there.

One final point on that would be around guaranteed standards for smart metering. We know that some people experience billing issues when their smart meter goes wrong. Ofgem has developed a guaranteed standard but not implemented it yet. We want to see that implemented as soon as possible. That would give people compensation if their smart meter is broken.

Torcuil Crichton: Nye, what goes wrong for people who rent?

Nye Jones: The most common issue we hear about is energy debt.

Torcuil Crichton: Alex mentioned that it is huge.

Nye Jones: Yes. Overall it has tripled since 2021 and now stands at around £5 billion. For private renters specifically, I spoke at the start about that vicious combination of unaffordable rents and high bills. In the short term, there is less impact on you of not paying your energy bill in full than there is of not paying your rent. Often renters in winter, when pressured, will pay their rent and forgo paying their bills. Some will not turn the heating on or go without food.

We often hear from younger people who are less aware of the process and keep the heating on, but then their bill goes up. They are also not aware of the interest that they will pay on the debt. Then it is like quicksand and it pulls you in. Some 54% of private renters have access to less than £500 in savings, so there is no way of getting out.

It was positive to see the Government publish their debt relief scheme. The key to that is properly funding it to make sure people can come out of that debt. What we are not in favour of, which I know Ofgem is consulting on at the moment, is the return of lessening the safeguards around prepayment meters. We do not think that that should be the answer. That can leave vulnerable people in really difficult situations where they cannot turn heating on in really cold homes.

Torcuil Crichton: Katie, thanks for your evidence and thanks for coming in. ECO4 is a massive scandal. Thanks for bringing it to us, although we are aware of it—

Dr Barrett: I am not sure you are fully aware of the scale, because the Government have not released any figures.

Torcuil Crichton: We have your evidence here, but clearly things have gone badly wrong—

Dr Barrett: There is a very big issue with safeguarding as well.

Torcuil Crichton: Can I speak, and then you? Things have gone badly wrong here. You have talked about companies liquidating to avoid responsibility and not being able to chase them. It is not just that the installation broke; the system to protect consumers broke as well, didn’t it?

Dr Barrett: Yes, completely.

Torcuil Crichton: Tell us how.

Dr Barrett: Let me quote three other victims. “Why are all the accreditation bodies so biased in favour of installers? TrustMark is the worst of them”. “TrustMark are not there to enforce standards. They are there to cover the backs of their fee-paying members.” “Why is TrustMark allowed to continue to be involved in rectifying the ECO4 damage it has presided over? Has Trustmark been investigated?” It is still telling people, “They’re not part of us. They’re not accredited by us any more, so we can’t do anything about it.” It is not fit for purpose. The fact that it has “trust” in its name is horrifying.

Another victim said: “What concrete action will the Government take to restore these families’ homes, compensate them for the harm suffered, and hold those responsible to account?” The guy who was the director of the company that did my install has another company that is still operating with the same director. He also has a company that rents out limos. He is not in the building trade; he is just an opportunist. He hired a bunch of plasterers and is bodging work and going off. The people who supposedly attended my property are not the people on the paperwork.

I have got a lot of information via a subject access request and it has been heavily redacted. Because the retrofit co-ordinator lost his job, he sent me a lot of unredacted information and that is how I know how much fraud has happened in my case in particular. The retrofit assessor on the paperwork is not the person who attended my property. The person who assessed my property is just some bloke called Barry who does not have any qualifications.

Honestly, they have destroyed my home, my health and my career. They have destroyed everything. I am not a typical victim. I am quite outspoken, shall we say, and very educated. I am vulnerable. That is why. I have health issues and stuff. There are a lot of people who cannot navigate the system. We are campaigners who have come together. There were five of us who met with Mr McCluskey in June. We are the ones who are fighting for all the little old ladies who were cold-called and have had this work done.

One of the other campaigners is renting. Every time it rains, it rains in her kitchen because of one of the vents they put in. They did not do it properly. There is mould everywhere and her landlord is doing nothing to help remediate it whatsoever. She has been doing all the work.

I reckon between us we could probably all do a PhD in the failings of ECO4. There is this whole thing, “Well, we have decided that we are going to do this foundation to help with it.” As far as I am aware, eight people have been referred. We presented 10 test cases to Martin McCluskey in June and asked him whether he could help people who have been through all of the process properly. They have followed all the complaints processes, which takes a very long time. Bear in mind that the guarantees for heating systems are only for two years; those have well elapsed. Not one of those 10 test cases—sorry, migraine brain struggling to do words—has been remediated.

Torcuil Crichton: There are 300,000 homes. If your home is destroyed, of course it affects your health. We can tell from your passionate presentation—

Dr Barrett: I had seizures at the end of 2024. I am not epileptic. They do not know what caused them. It is horrifying.

Torcuil Crichton: Very quickly, what is the fix you want the Minister to do?

Dr Barrett: I want him to do it properly. There is a lot of obscurity about the figures. I do not think that they are going into people’s houses. Well, they are not. TrustMark is doing audits and supposedly it has done 9,000, but we have not seen the evidence of that. It is doing desktop audits based on data that is not correct.

I know for a fact that the data that relates to my installation is completely fake. There are photographs dated months after they left. There is a photograph of a storage heater that never existed, which they put on the wall to take a photo of to say that it was there, so that they could take it away. It was a way of increasing the amount of money they could get out of British Gas.

Torcuil Crichton: Presumably they took it from house to house.

Dr Barrett: Yes, apparently so, because it happened to several other people.

Chair: We will have to end it there.

Torcuil Crichton: Thank you all for coming in.

Chair: Can I thank all of you for your evidence? It has been extremely valuable in the context of not just today’s short inquiry but our longer inquiry into warm and comfortable homes. We will pursue the evidence that you have given us with Ofgem, the ombudsman and the Minister, not just today but in future inquiries.

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Ed Dodman and Neil Kenward.

Chair: Welcome back to this morning’s session of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee on preparing for winter. We welcome Ed Dodman and Neil Kenward from, respectively, the Energy Ombudsman and Ofgem. Gentlemen, you both sat there listening to the same evidence that we did. What is your reaction to what you heard?

Ed Dodman: Clearly, all three of the witnesses were concerned about the winter coming up, for different reasons. We are too, and are monitoring the situation closely. Price has always been the best predictor of complaints coming to the ombudsman. When prices went up significantly during the energy crisis, complaints to our service were not far off doubling within two years. We peaked at about 120,000 in 2023. We are currently at about 90,000, so we are not at the level we were, but we are monitoring very closely.

Katie’s testimony was very affecting. The ECO4 and the low-carbon technology space is not an area we currently cover. Indeed, it is very difficult having to turn away consumers who come to us thinking that we can help.

Chair: Do you think it is an area that you should cover?

Ed Dodman: It is a very complicated area today for consumers to navigate. It is complicated for us in the sector sometimes to understand. There is an argument for making things simpler for consumers. We support the idea of a warm homes ombudsman. That of course covers only publicly funded installations and improvements. We think that it is a sector that could absolutely be simplified. We could play a role in providing dispute resolution for consumers in some of these situations. They think we do today and, as I say, it is very difficult in some situations to turn them away.

The added complication of that is that sometimes a consumer does not know what the problem is. They might come to us with a problem on their bill or perhaps they are not seeing the savings that they thought they might get from some of the low-carbon technology. If it is a problem with the energy supply, we can help today, but of course the consumer does not know that. If it turns out to be a problem with their technology, unfortunately that does not fall within our remit. It is absolutely an area that can be simplified and strengthened for consumers.

Chair: Neil, I have the same question for you. There was plenty of reference to Ofgem in the last session.

Neil Kenward: Yes, of course. We heard some very powerful testimony there and evidence on some of the problems that consumers have experienced. We look also at the winter ahead and recognise that, with energy bills likely to rise significantly in January, this will cause serious and significant problems for a number of energy consumers, both households and businesses. We are preparing. We are monitoring the situation closely. Beyond that, we have robust rules in place that the energy suppliers must follow. We are working with them now to understand that they are ready to do that and prepared for the winter that is coming.

Chair: You have not commented on Katie’s testimony.

Neil Kenward: As I say, it was powerful testimony. Clearly there have been serious, fundamental problems with the ECO4 programme. There is a find and fix programme that the Government lead on. It is their role and their responsibility with TrustMark. We are supportive of everything they are trying to do to remedy the problems.

Chair: What is Ofgem’s role with the response to the failings of ECO4?

Neil Kenward: Let me set out how the roles are organised between us. The role of DESNZ is one of policy. It determines the programme of ECO4. We are the administrators of the programme. We check that the obligations on suppliers to deliver a certain number of interventions are met. Then the quality assurance around those, I believe, sits with TrustMark.

There have been differential responsibilities. We went beyond our formal role when these problems emerged—

Chair: Sorry to interrupt, but if your formal role is to administer the scheme, anybody hearing that would suggest that you have a responsibility and that there is an accountability for your role. How do you apply that accountability?

Neil Kenward: It is quite a narrow role. Our key function is essentially to ensure that the suppliers deliver the number of interventions that they are meant to be delivering.

Chair: Without reference to the quality.

Neil Kenward: That is not formally our role. As I was saying, we stepped beyond our formal role when these issues started to emerge. We set up a dedicated call centre that still operates.

Chair: You did not do it very well, judging by what Katie has just told us.

Neil Kenward: I would be very happy to follow up with Katie and understand the individual case and, indeed, the ones she referenced. The find and fix programme is the main vehicle, and that is a DESNZ trademark programme that is, I believe, trying to find and fix, as it sets out. I recognise that the process is going slower than we would all want.

Chair: Which, in the run-up to winter, is really serious.

Neil Kenward: It absolutely is.

Mike Reader: Just for my clarity, is the find and fix programme administered by DESNZ or Ofgem?

Neil Kenward: It is not administered by Ofgem. It is a DESNZ programme working with TrustMark.

Mike Reader: So DESNZ leads. We can ask the Minister, but he will have a team that runs that.

Neil Kenward: That is my—yes.

Mike Reader: What is your role in the find and fix programme?

Neil Kenward: We do not have a formal role in the find and fix programme. We are supporting with advice and with the contact centre. We ran our own audit. Obviously, we supported and oversaw the audits by TrustMark.

Mike Reader: In ECO4, you were responsible for administering the scheme and checking that things had been done from a numbers perspective, but you do not have any role in fixing the problem that has been created.

Neil Kenward: That is correct.

Mike Reader: I want to talk a bit about complaints. Do you see an uptick in complaints during winter?

Ed Dodman: Typically, quarter on quarter, we do not see an enormous change in the number of complaints. Obviously, because of where we sit in the process, sometimes what we see is delayed because companies have a chance to resolve complaints before they come to us.

As I indicated in my first answer, the biggest driver of the volume of complaints, certainly over the past few years, has been the price of energy. That, in our view, is for two reasons. First, it typically increases the amount of contact consumers raise with suppliers and complaints. Obviously, that can increase the number that come through to us. Secondly, as the price goes up, it makes it more important to people. What some people might have been willing to let lie means a lot more to people when the price goes up, especially if they are struggling in other situations.

When prices go up, we do not even necessarily see an uptick in particular types of complaints. We see a general increase in the propensity of people to come to us. This is potentially one of the most significant price rises we have seen for a long time, so we will be monitoring things very closely. We are in a good position to deal with that as an organisation. Consumers are currently waiting less time for us to resolve complaints than they have for a long time.

Neil Kenward: We track complaints. We measure them in the industry. We have tracked them every quarter since 2014, and there has been a steady downward trajectory in complaints. There have obviously been increases, particularly at points of high prices, as Ed suggests. We would not be surprised if there were an increase in complaints, but right now they are at the lowest level that we have ever tracked. Obviously, that is welcome. We would like to see them lower.

Mike Reader: Why do you think that is?

Neil Kenward: We have been working with the industry to try to drive up standards. We have put in robust requirements and monitored them. We engage with the suppliers who have the worst performance and, through our engagement with them and our compliance activity, require them to tackle the problems that come up most frequently.

Mike Reader: Do you see a different type of complaint depending on the time of year, or is it similar issues throughout?

Ed Dodman: I can give the ombudsman’s perspective. The categories of complaints do not change significantly from month to month. Lots of consumers pay on direct debit, and we see the same sorts of issues around things such as billing throughout the year. Billing has been for the past few years and remains our largest complaint category. It accounts for about 60% of cases. That has not increased, relatively speaking, compared with other complaints.

Neil Kenward: Billing remains the top issue as well for complaints before they reach the Energy Ombudsman stage. They are declining over time with complaints as a whole. The spread of smart meters and the upgrades of a lot of the energy companies’ systems are improving billing accuracy, but it is a slow process.

Mike Reader: Turning to debt, could you remind us of the current level of consumer fuel debt in the UK?

Neil Kenward: Ofgem measures it as unpaid bills after 91 days or more, and under that measure it is now over £5 billion. As Nye said, that is about three times what it was at the beginning of this decade, so that is a significant problem. We recognise that it is a problem for the people struggling to pay their bills. It also increases costs for everyone else because the costs of that bad debt need to be recovered.

Mike Reader: Do you think the Government have a coherent strategy to pay off that debt?

Neil Kenward: The Government, with Ofgem, published a major strategy to tackle and, over time, reduce energy debt. We did that alongside the Budget. It has a set of measures: relief, repayment and reform. The debt relief scheme is now moving ahead, as we have heard. Repayment is to try to ensure that customers are helped on to sustainable repayment plans, and that is the easy default to minimise debt accumulation in the first place. Reform is to make sure that the rules are suitable and to minimise the risks of debt accumulating, for example in the home moves process, which I can talk about more in detail if needed.

Mike Reader: Do you think we will get a handle on the debt and see it paid off within my lifetime?

Neil Kenward: I am confident that this package of measures will substantially reduce energy debt over time. To manage expectations, it will take time for those measures to take effect. In the short run, as energy bills go up, inevitably we are likely to see energy debt increase this winter, which is obviously troubling.

Mike Reader: Ed, do you think the Government have a clear strategy to pay off that debt?

Ed Dodman: Our role is to resolve issues that come to us. We do not take an organisational view on the merits of things such as debt write-off, but we will make sure that companies properly apply whatever policy is put in place.

Chair: Neil, you talked about changes to billing. What sorts of changes are customers saying to you that they want to see? You are coming to the end of your consultation, so you must have a pretty good idea of what people are asking for.

Neil Kenward: The critical thing is that consumers can have an accurate, timely bill that they understand and can engage with, so that they understand how much energy they are utilising and how much that is costing them. We are moving towards an outcomes-based form of regulation, which Alex mentioned on the previous panel, where we are going to really focus on those objectives to make sure that the billing process delivers what consumers need.

Chair: Okay, and a bill that people can understand.

Neil Kenward: Energy can be complex. We have not got it entirely right in the industry in terms of making sure every bill is something that every consumer can engage with effectively.

Chair: Can I ask you about back billing? We have been hearing that retailers are using people’s credit balances to fund back billing while inquiries are going on. Do you think that is right?

Neil Kenward: Back billing remains a problem. It is reducing. We have introduced quite robust rules to protect consumers from back billing. Any energy that enters a bill that was consumed more than 12 months ago can no longer be recovered from consumers.

Chair: The question was about accumulated credit.

Neil Kenward: If a customer has an accumulated credit balance, they have the right to request that back at any time, so the energy company is not essentially borrowing off the consumer. That is a rule that is also in place.

Chair: So you do not regard the use of accumulated credit as legitimate in the case of back billing.

Neil Kenward: Yes, the use of consumer credit is primarily for direct debit customers to smooth the annual payments to make them constant month by month.

Chair: Ed, in any cases that come to you, would you give the same ruling?

Ed Dodman: Yes. The connection between consumer credit and back billing is not one that we see materialise commonly. Back billing is a small but very significant issue for those affected. It accounts for about 5% of the complaints that we receive, so, although it is very serious, it is less common proportionally.

It is an area that is more serious, though. We typically award a greater level of compensation for consumers who have been through back billing than we might for other types of complaints. It is a very significant issue for those people, and of course it can be very meaningful in terms of the amounts that people are being asked to pay.

Neil Kenward: Since we introduced that rule, there have been a million customers who have benefited from that. Collectively, £172 million has been written off by suppliers because they were asking for it too late. This is a really powerful incentive for energy companies to bill accurately and in a timely fashion.

Chair: Do you agree with our recommendation that the time period should be six months rather than 12?

Neil Kenward: That is definitely something we will be considering as we look through. As I say, we are looking at a billing consumer outcome and how we can deliver the best standards for consumers going forward. We will be publishing on that in due course.

Ed Dodman: I do not want to give another boring answer. That is probably a question for Ofgem. We have lots of evidence that will help inform that decision, around how people have been asked to pay bills, sometimes from many years ago, never mind six or 12 months ago.

Chair: That was not a boring answer at all.

Graeme Downie: Just picking up on some of the broader themes from the last panel, neither of you is from an advocacy body as such, but we heard last time about the difficulties disadvantaged groups have with getting redress and information, whether that is people with disabilities, people who have health conditions or people who are in crisis. How much do you see your job as actively standing up for consumers from those backgrounds rather than simply being available and passive?

Neil Kenward: We are very keenly aware that part of our job is to ensure that vulnerable consumers are protected and treated fairly and with respect. We have rules that the energy suppliers must follow to engage appropriately and supportively with vulnerable consumers. There is a whole host of protections in place in the energy supply licence.

Graeme Downie: Are you relying on people being able to come to you?

Neil Kenward: We do not deal with individual cases of vulnerable consumers. We set the rules that the suppliers must then follow. If the suppliers are failing to do that properly, we will follow up, investigate and, if necessary, take action.

Ed Dodman: We are not officially a consumer advocate, but we exist because there is a problem, which is that consumers often do not get the redress that they deserve. I would consider us an advocate in terms of advocating for access to our service, absolutely. We try to make it as easy as possible for people from all sorts of backgrounds to use us. There is no doubt that it can be a very daunting process for people to undertake. Ombudsmen can have a perceived sense of formality and a judicial perspective that can put people off.

Graeme Downie: What actions do you take to reduce that and to make people feel like you are actually, if not an advocate, at least on their side or there to help them to seek redress?

Ed Dodman: There are two things. One is how we make our service accessible. A few years ago, we implemented a single case owner from start to finish in the process. The person who accepts your complaint today will be the person who deals with it from start to finish until it closes. That allows us to understand whether you might have additional support needs that we might need to cater for.

We offer a variety of communication channels and different languages. We can allow you more time if you are in a difficult situation. We can allow people to advocate on your behalf for the case.

Graeme Downie: I want to pick up on that last point in just a second.

When it comes to the single caseworker, is that something that you manage to retain throughout all cases, given staffing changes? What percentage of cases have the same caseworker from beginning to end?

Ed Dodman: I do not know the specific answer to that question, which I would be happy to take away.

Graeme Downie: That would be helpful. I appreciate that that is the right path, but it has to be something that is being achieved.

Ed Dodman: Exactly. One circumstance would be if, like you say, someone is taken ill or goes on holiday. The other circumstance is where a consumer or a supplier has decided to appeal our case. We offer that opportunity in certain circumstances, and we do not think it is right that the same person would review that case, so that would also happen in those cases.

Graeme Downie: Can I pick up your point about helping a sibling or a family member—or, dare I say it, an MP’s caseworker getting in touch on someone’s behalf? How easy is it for that person to deal with the ombudsman and advocate on behalf of their relative, friend or constituent?

Ed Dodman: If someone gives you permission to raise your case and deal with it on their behalf, it should be as easy for you as for the other.

Graeme Downie: How is that done? Having dealt with other public bodies, I know that often it has to be a wet signature delivered by pigeon post on a certain day between the hours of 12.01 and 12.02.

Ed Dodman: That is not the case for us.

Graeme Downie: Can you explain how you approach that?

Ed Dodman: It depends on the way the consumer wants to communicate with us. We do not try to add in extra delay through things such as requiring a hard signature to do that. If an MP or their team raises a case on someone’s behalf, we will do our diligence to make sure they have the authority to do it on behalf of consumers, but, once we are sure that the consumer wants to go down that path, we try to make it as easy as possible.

Graeme Downie: Is it a phone call? Is it a bit of paper?

Ed Dodman: It will depend on the channel that the consumer wants to engage with us on.

Graeme Downie: Can it be as easy as, say, an email tick box?

Ed Dodman: I would need to take that away and check how it works on the system.

Graeme Downie: Again, it would be good to know.

Ed Dodman: I would be very happy to provide some more information on that.

Graeme Downie: Thank you. We know that people from disadvantaged backgrounds are underrepresented among complaints or issues raised. Are there better ways we can measure that so we know what is being missed? How do we measure what is being missed?

Ed Dodman: We survey the consumers who choose to use our service and we ask them things such as demographic questions. As you would expect, we under-index on some of the characteristics that you are alluding to. Socioeconomic background is something we under-index on. This is something we are very conscious of.

We support the measures that the Government are introducing through their fairer, faster redress decisions. That should help not only vulnerable customers but all customers come to us.

One thing would be the reduced waiting time for suppliers. Currently, if you raised a complaint with a supplier today, the supplier would have until mid-January to resolve it before they bring it to us. We think that is too long, and we are glad that the Government have reduced it.

Another thing would be standardised signposting—making sure that consumers are told about us in the same way, regardless of who their company is. These are all things that might help level the playing field for consumers who might otherwise find it difficult to come to us.

Graeme Downie: Neil, how joined up is the work you are doing with Scottish bodies in particular, bearing in mind that there are differences in consumer advocates and everything else, and in how things come through? How does Ofgem approach that work with Scottish bodies versus the rest of the UK?

Neil Kenward: We engage with them on an equal and frequent basis.

Graeme Downie: Does having the two create any additional friction or any difficulties in process? How is that managed?

Neil Kenward: I do not think so. We think it is hugely important that we are a GB-wide regulator, so we absolutely engage with Scottish and, where appropriate, Welsh authorities as well.

Claire Young: Neil, how serious would a consumer issue have to be for a retailer to risk losing their licence? If that were to happen, what are the steps that would happen before you removed it?

Neil Kenward: It is quite a step-by-step process. We set very clear rules. We then monitor compliance with those rules across the sector. Where we see things going wrong, we get reports of that, and we have lots of ways of picking up that intelligence.

We will then engage with the supplier. We will give it an opportunity to fix the problem, and then if that is not adequately done, we will move to enforcement, which will usually result, if the supplier is found not to have complied with their obligations, in significant fines.

We also have rules that can limit the ability of individual executives to work in the sector; it is called the fit and proper regime. If people have been found to take decisions that are very much against the rules and against consumer interests, we can take steps to stop them working in the sector in future.

Claire Young: This year, you have not issued any fines.

Neil Kenward: We have issued a number of fines. We have issued the largest redress package that we have ever done in a retail market.

Claire Young: You have issued redress payments, but that is a different thing from fines.

Neil Kenward: There were penalties in addition. Fines is an option. We usually agree a contribution to the voluntary redress fund. Technically, it is not called a fine; it is a penalty. It is a very similar thing in terms of its actual impact—millions of pounds of costs for the energy supplier. Suppliers pay a significant price as well as compensating the consumers who have suffered from whatever action they suffered.

Claire Young: What do you think an acceptable level of failure by retailers is?

Neil Kenward: There is no acceptable level of failure. We take action, and I am delighted to say that customer satisfaction is at record levels in the sector. Complaints are at the lowest they have been. I am not pretending that we are in a perfect situation; we are certainly not. We are working with consumer groups, charities and, indeed, the companies themselves to drive standards higher, and we will continue to do so.

Claire Young: For example, if someone is being billed £100 too much, that is an absolute pittance to the retailer, but for a family in fuel poverty it could mean switching off their heating. Do you think that your penalties on retailers when it comes to billing mistakes actually reflect the impact on the customer?

Neil Kenward: We have a rule of thumb around the consumer harm that is suffered and therefore the amount of restitution or compensation that is required. Sometimes the issue is not one that is easily measurable in pounds, but we will require some degree of compensation along with that.

Claire Young: How are you recognising that?

Neil Kenward: We try to assess the level of harm suffered by the individual and then a commensurate sum of money to compensate them for that.

Claire Young: Given the widespread use of smart meters now, surely every retailer should just be able to achieve accurate bills for customers within 12 months. Do you think there is a lack of ambition to end the problems with billing?

Neil Kenward: I am disappointed that there has not been greater progress. The issue is improving over time, but it remains the area of greatest complaint. I can say that that 12-month rule on back billing has resulted in millions of pounds being written off because the suppliers had not billed in a timely way. That in itself is a very powerful incentive for them to get their billing systems improved, which most of them are in the process of doing or have done.

Claire Young: Ed, the ombudsman role is much more limited, but what are your thoughts on the level of ambition to end billing problems?

Ed Dodman: As a positive reflection, this, in my view, is one of the areas that companies are really focusing on. Billing is an issue for us. It is an even bigger issue for companies. On the whole, companies are trying to make things simpler and more understandable for customers.

It is not surprising that it remains the largest cause of complaints. For most people, it is their only interaction with their supplier. Most people would like to pay their bill and forget about it, so it is perhaps not surprising that it is the example that comes out in complaints the most. I share Neil’s aspiration for it to continue to improve, but I see positive signs in the industry that suppliers are doing what they can to make things as simple as possible for consumers.

Claire Young: Do you have an idea of an acceptable level of failure and where the level of failure is in relation to that?

Ed Dodman: It is difficult to put a number on it. As you can imagine, performance varies a lot from supplier to supplier. There are external factors in the market that drive complaint volumes as well. I have already talked about price. Some of those are outside of company controls.

Our job is to make sure that, when something does happen, it is put right. We have awarded over £9 million to consumers so far this year in compensation payments or what we call time and trouble awards. That is on top of any remedial activity we have required of companies. We try to reflect the stress that individual issues have caused for consumers.

Wera Hobhouse: Increasingly, constituents feel empowered to write to MPs using AI. At the same time, they do not actually want an AI response; they want somebody real behind their complaint. Can you outline how much you are using AI in your operations?

Ed Dodman: Like you, we are seeing it from consumers as well. The length of evidence and case file we are getting now is very clearly being influenced by AI.

We are committed to retaining a human-centred approach to our resolution service. The last thing people want to do, probably, is talk to another bot when they come to us, having potentially been through that in their complaint. However, we are using AI, for example, to make accessing the rules and regulations simpler for our people, to improve quality in our organisation and to pre-judge where we might be able to strengthen our decisions.
