It is very much an enabler for us. We do not see it ever replacing the human-to-human contact that people want when they are in that sort of situation.

Neil Kenward: Likewise, we are using AI to enable improved productivity and efficiency in Ofgem, but all our products have to be responsible and accountable to individual humans who will be assuring the quality of what we do and publish. That will be the case.

The biggest opportunity for us is making better use of data. There is a growing amount of data in the sector. We are finding the right ways to gather that data. We are using AI, for example, to better gather and analyse that information so that we can become a more effective regulator.

Chair: Thank you very much for your evidence this morning, Ed Dodman and Neil Kenward.

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Martin McCluskey, David Thomas and Ben Golding.

Chair: Welcome back to this morning’s session of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee. Minister Martin McCluskey, welcome. You are joined by two colleagues from the Department, who I will ask to introduce themselves, please.

Ben Golding: Good morning. I am Ben Golding. I am the director of affordability and retail at the Department.

David Thomas: I am David Thomas. I am the interim director general for household consumers and energy retail.

Chair: Thank you all for joining us. Minister, have you been briefed by your officials on what we heard in the first panel?

Martin McCluskey: In part, yes.

Chair: Would you like me to put some of the more compelling parts of the evidence to you?

Martin McCluskey indicated assent.

Chair: First, on ECO4, we have had evidence in the past, and we have had really quite harrowing evidence again this morning, about the failings, but also the failure to respond to them and the fact that 100,000 people are still suffering the consequences of poorly installed measures, including insulation, very often leading to them living in damp, cold homes with significant health problems and, indeed, structural problems as well.

We have published reports on this in the past, and we are reminded that not much has changed, if anything, including that a group met you, Minister, in June and have seen no action since. Accreditation has been removed from multiple installers, but the removal of that accreditation means that there is now no accountability for their actions, and the removal of that accreditation has not led to remedial works being carried out.

These are really significant and worrying allegations, including the implication of a lack of action by the Department in an area for which you are responsible. How do you respond?

Martin McCluskey: Thank you for the opportunity to come this morning and also to address this point, because it was something that I was hoping there would be an opportunity to respond to.

Let me take you back to September 2025, when I started, at that point in the energy consumers brief. It was either day one or day two in the role, and I was presented at that point with a draft copy of the National Audit Office’s report into ECO4, which had the 98% failure rate in EWI reported in it. It would be an understatement to say that I was shocked by what was in that report and the extent of the failure in that scheme.

In reading it, there was obviously a lot of work done by my predecessor at that point—the now Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero—who had started work before the National Audit Office reported to look at how we might be able to help and remediate. What was so shocking about it was the lack of oversight in the scheme. That was in large part the reason why the ECO4 scheme was ended.

There is some remediation happening at the moment, but we are no longer fitting new measures under ECO4. The scheme had clearly failed. It did not have correct oversight. A scheme that originally, under ECO1, had started supplying LED lightbulbs and draught excluders to people had then extended into a scheme that was installing quite complex measures in people’s homes: EWI, SWI, heat pumps, solar panels and batteries. It was a much more complicated scheme than was originally intended.

There are a number of things that we have done over that year. At the time of the publication of the NAO report—in October 2025—I made a written ministerial statement to Parliament laying out what we would do to find and fix those cases in the 98% failure rate within ECO—to fix those cases but, most importantly, find them.

I will just take the Committee through some numbers. There were 24,600 in that population that we were looking to remediate. So far, every property in that population has been contacted by Ofgem. They will have received a letter from Ofgem with the proposal for audit, because we cannot fix something until we know what the problems are. TrustMark then makes up to three contacts to people within that population. So far, TrustMark has contacted 19,216 people. We have completed 11,141 audits, and we have completed 2,227 remediations on that population. There have been people who, when contacted, have either refused or not picked up the phone. There are about 4,000 people in that population who we have not been able to contact.

There is another thing we have done with this EWI population, because there are particular hotspots within that 98% failure rate, particularly in places such as Leicester and Luton. In Leicester and Luton, we have recruited people from within the community to go door by door to find and communicate with the individuals we believe to be affected so that we can reach them. That has certainly had some success in driving up the audit rates. That is one thing we have done in terms of the find and fix.

DESNZ also worked with the voluntary redress fund and the Energy Saving Trust to put in place a scheme that those people who have run out of routes for redress can now apply to. We have enough funding in that for about 170 cases to be covered, and that is progressing at the moment. That is what we have done so far on the backward-looking piece.

On the forward-looking piece around future schemes, as I said, we have already cancelled the ECO scheme. It was right that we did that because of the levels of failure. We consulted from June to September on a new model of consumer protection. I hope that we are going to have the Government response to that out quite soon, in order to put in place a system where the kinds of failures that we saw during ECO never happen again.

That consultation will set out a much simpler system and route for redress for people. That is really important, because for those people—not just the individuals I met in June, but other people I have met over the course of the last year who have been deeply affected by this—the commitment the Government have to make is not just that we will fix the problem, but that we will make sure that this does not happen to anyone again in the future.

It is the case that we inherited this system. I do not want to sound like I am making a political point around this, but ECO4 was not our scheme. ECO4 was the scheme of the last Conservative Government. In delivering our schemes at the moment, I always have in my head that we cannot end up with something as fragmented and as failing as we had with ECO4.

In the role that I am in now, taking responsibility for the future system, especially now that we start thinking about the devolution of the warm homes plan—we will probably talk about that later—it is essential that we have a system in place before devolution in 2028 that is going to adequately protect people. I am quite confident, with what we are doing through the Department in terms of the schemes that are in place now, that we would not see the kind of failure rate that we saw in ECO, because we have much greater oversight of the schemes that we are operating, which are now largely being operated through local government.

Chair: We want to get on to this winter as much as we can, but this is too important to not pursue further. I would like to ask the officials about how we got here in the first place before the change of Government.

Before I do that, you gave some figures: 11,141 audits, 2,227 remedials, refusal or lack of response from 4,000, and 170 cases covered by the redress scheme. I think I have noted those down accurately. We heard a figure of 100,000 people affected; that is a big gap with any of those figures.

Martin McCluskey: We have to disaggregate the population here. We made a commitment to those people who were affected by the problems with solid wall insulation, particularly external wall insulation, that we would find and fix their problem. That is the population of 24,600 that I mentioned a moment ago. I myself would not recognise the figure of 100,000, but we are obviously aware of other cases within ECO where there is remediation required.

Just to be very clear about it, I am not going to sit here and defend the system that this Government were not responsible for establishing, which is why we are changing it. The way the system is meant to work is that the installers who install faulty measures are the ones who repair and remediate any problems in the system. The guarantee providers who stand behind that provide guarantees that, if that fails, there is some level of insurance behind it. It is clear that in some cases that has not operated, which is why we are changing the system for the future. I really want to stress this point: we have ended ECO4 and the schemes that we have in place right now are very different from the ones before.

There will be a population of people who are not covered by the specific find and fix measures that we have set out who will require remediation, but for whom the system needs to provide some level of remediation. The commitment that I can give here is that we have already set up a complex cases unit within the Department that is looking at some of the most complex cases. It is the case that many people who have issues within ECO get their problems remediated. For those complex cases, we have officials who are looking at them to help guide people through what is a ridiculously complicated process of trying to get remediation. The reason why we have set that up and we have that function is that we recognise that people often need some support to take themselves through that.

For this 24,600, and for all of them who come forward who we audit, we will then fix. We have the VRF scheme, which is obviously not our scheme, but through the Energy Saving Trust it will hopefully try to deal with some of the most extreme cases where, for example, suppliers have gone bust or we have run out of road in the system. We will continue to look at what more might be required. For the future system, we have stopped ECO and, in the future, there will be a new system of consumer protection.

Chair: There is also criticism made by the industry that there is a lack of understanding of what comes next. This is causing them a real problem. Those suppliers and installers who are reputable are really struggling because of this gap. What can you say to them about giving them certainty of work to come? Equally, that in part is about rebuilding consumer confidence in the warm homes plan.

Martin McCluskey: I would say two things. The point you made at the end there, Chair, about maintaining confidence is really important. We are asking people in the warm homes plan to upgrade their homes. We are hoping to reach 5 million home upgrades by the end of this Parliament. For some people, that will be through the future homes standard and regulation will take care of it. For others, we are asking them to retrofit and to take that action. We need to maintain confidence in the system.

I have heard from Members of Parliament and from installers directly. I have a lot of sympathy for those good installers who have done the right thing and maybe were not involved in the failures of ECO. We have begun to set out what devolution will mean, and I have been very clear with installers. I met some representative groups recently. We are working with the mayors and the installers to look, in areas where mayors will take on responsibility, at what they can be doing now, ahead of 2028, to start to build up local supply chains.

I have been very clear about what the direction of travel is, but at the front of my mind has to be how we protect consumers and how we make sure that the kinds of examples that you will have heard this morning around the failure of ECO never happen again. For me, that has to be the primary objective. If that means, unfortunately, that in some areas we have to pause and take stock before we move on to the next stage of devolution, we have to do that.

Just to address the installer point directly, there is a lot of work out there already. Maybe we can come on to this in a bit more detail later. Devolution will allow local authorities, strategic authorities and mayoral authorities to build up their own local supply chains, which presents a much better opportunity for SME installers to access opportunities through Government schemes. We have heard a lot that tier 1 contractors are sucking up a lot of the work. I want to make sure that SMEs and local supply chains get a benefit from the work the Government are doing.

Chair: You mentioned 2028. That is a long way away for installers. I am talking to installers who are reputable, and I think my colleagues are too. They have a good record already and are now being held back. I have a constituent who is in this situation. He has invested in a training facility and now the money is not being released, so he cannot carry out any of the work, and it is really hitting his business viability.

Martin McCluskey: I would maybe look at it a little differently from saying the money is not being released. Next year, there will be well over £1 billion being put through Government schemes, so there is a significant amount of money going out now and in the next financial year.

It is a very different scheme from ECO. As you will all be aware, the way that the ECO scheme ran is that an obligation was put on energy suppliers. The energy suppliers then went and found the businesses. The contracts were between the energy suppliers and the SMEs, and they went off and they installed measures on people’s homes and then reported back to Ofgem.

Going back to where we started on this line of questioning, we have stopped that because that did not provide us with enough oversight. That means that there will be more hoops to jump through, bluntly, in order to get access to Government schemes, but that is right because of the failings that we have seen through a system such as ECO.

We are working on this in a very different way, but there is over £1 billion programmed to go out in the next financial year. There is around the same or slightly less in this financial year, going out at the moment. Our schemes are working at full pelt. We are fully committed in terms of our budget for this year and next year, and there is a lot of work out there.

We have done work with installers. We have done work with local supply chains, and also with the tier 1 contractors to ensure that the tier 1 contractors are opening up their work to small businesses across the country. We will continue to push that.

We have put conditions in some of our schemes to ensure that those tier 1 contractors open it up to local contractors as well. Unfortunately, the truth at the moment is that, because we have stopped ECO, there is going to be this gap, but we have stopped ECO for the right reasons and for the reasons given by the witnesses you heard this morning.

Chair: I want to ask one more question on this before we start to move on; my colleagues have lots of questions as well. It is to the officials—probably David. Why was this allowed to become such a massive problem? We heard about a plasterer being used to install solid wall insulation on top of damp walls. Why was this happening on an industrial scale? How did that end up happening?

David Thomas: As the Minister has said, clearly what happened is not at all what should have happened. Lots of these cases are really distressing. As the Department and other colleagues have said in other forums, the Department took its eye off the ball. We did not set up a system that had clear enough accountability, and, exactly as the Minister has been saying, this is therefore the sort of thing that we need to fix going forward. The system was not set up with appropriate oversight.

Chair: David, with the greatest of respect, we know what happened, but why? What was going on? What was the system and the culture that meant that these things were allowed to happen? That is the learning so it never happens again.

David Thomas: There are lots of things that have gone wrong, obviously. The key learning that I take from it is accountability. If you turn the clock back to when the system was originally set up and envisaged in this way, the idea was that there should be a higher standard of protection. That was the aim of bringing in PAS 2035 and having TrustMark oversee it. In practice, we have seen that that clearly did not work.

Also, there was a lack of clarity and accountability. Who was overseeing who? Who was responsible for the work? There is a long list of things I could add to that that have gone wrong in practice. The single most important thing we need to do in setting up the new consumer protection framework is to ensure that there is not that lack of clarity going forward.

Mike Reader: Minister, on the point that David has raised, what work have you and your predecessors done to go and root out the problem that led to this? It is quite clear to me that this is another case of the state ignoring victims when they were raising it early. Before the scheme got to 99% failure, there were people raising this repeatedly to Government, and they were completely ignored by the state. What are you doing to make sure that the Department changes, and particularly, if those civil servants were found to have acted inappropriately, that there is redress and that that is dealt with by your Department?

Martin McCluskey: I will take that in two parts. First, on what we have learned, we have learned a lot from our own work, but we have also learned a lot from the work that the NAO has done. We have learned a lot from what the PAC and this Committee have done.

Part of the reason why we have set up the system for complex cases within the Department, as I outlined a moment ago, is that we recognise that the stress that people have been put under over the years has been unbearable, and that they need significant support all the way through. That is one major lesson that has been learned through that. That was learned before I came into this role in September 2025. Miatta did a lot of this work, and I am not going to take credit for all of it. That is one specific thing that we learned.

I go back to the point that we have ended ECO. The biggest learning was that ECO was a failing scheme. To build on what David said a moment ago, my analysis of this is that the lack of oversight was born of the fact that the system was established where individual energy companies were contracting with SMEs. David talked about PAS 2035 being there as a standard, but it clearly was not being audited properly.

When we have looked at our current schemes and what we are doing for the future, but also what we are doing with anything being installed right now, there is a really high-quality audit regime in place now, which was actually in place under local government schemes that were running at the same time as ECO, but the standard was a lot higher in the local government schemes than they were through ECO.

I go back to the point I made at the very beginning. The ECO system was set up under the last Labour Government to do things like hand out LED lightbulbs and to give people draught excluders. That may have been an appropriate structure to deliver that kind of scheme; it was not the way to deliver heat pumps, solar, batteries and solid wall insulation.

Mike Reader: Ofgem was very clear with us in the previous panel that it was accountable for audit. You have just told us that audit was not good enough. Would you accept that Ofgem failed here? What changes have you asked for from Ofgem to make sure that, if it has a role in administering future schemes, we do not see this happen again?

Martin McCluskey: There have clearly been failures. I said a moment ago that I am not going to sit here and defend the system that delivered that level of failure. There have clearly been failures in Ofgem. There have been failures in other parts of the system. As I said, we consulted on consumer protection. We are in the process at the moment of putting together the Government response, and I hope to have that out soon.

Mike Reader: Do you have confidence in Ofgem?

Martin McCluskey: I am just going to go back to what I said a moment ago, Mike. There have clearly been failures in the system. We are designing a system now. Ofgem, post the Ofgem review, is a very different organisation from what it was a number of years ago.

The most important thing now is that we put a system in place for the future through the Government response to the consumer protection consultation, which, as I said, will come out soon. We are learning all those lessons from the last few years and putting something in place that makes sure this never happens again.

Chair: We heard an example of somebody going to Ofgem and being told to go to DESNZ, and going to DESNZ and being told to go to Ofgem. Why is that still happening?

Martin McCluskey: It should not be happening. That is the reason why the complex cases system was established, because people were being sent from pillar to post. If there are examples of that still happening now, I would like to hear about them. I know that was happening a year ago because I was hearing that from people, but if that is still happening now I want to hear about it, because it should not be, given what we have set up to try to deal with it.

Chair: You may have the opportunity to hear about them at the end of the session, Minister. We encourage you to do so.

Cornwall Insight is predicting a 26% rise in the price cap in January. It has been pretty consistent in the accuracy of its predictions. We heard that the average bill will be £200 higher between January and March 2027 than it was in 2026, and that the £100 is not targeted, especially for those people in private rented accommodation, in particular those in shared properties. That is the evidence we heard earlier. What is your response to those comments?

Martin McCluskey: For anyone in DESNZ and anyone working on this at the moment, the cost of energy is weighing heavily on all of us—Ministers and officials. That is why we have taken a really concerted effort to act over the last year.

None of this is to diminish the impact that rises in energy prices are going to have on people, but it is important to note what we have done as a Government over the last year. In the last Budget in 2025, we removed the renewables obligation from energy bills, saving people money. We ended ECO. That took money off bills. We now have the warm home discount, with a £150 discount extended to 6 million households, which was a significant extension that this Government put in place. We have the 0% VAT and now also the £100 support for those people in council tax bands A to D.

I am not going to sit here and pretend that that is going to alleviate for everyone the pressure that will be felt over this winter, but for those households, and certainly those most vulnerable households, there is a significant amount of support on offer, much of which will come automatically to them and they do not need to apply to, in order to keep it simple. It is obviously something we will continue to keep under review.

What I would say about bands A to D, to take on some of the comments you made a moment ago, is that there is no perfect way to reach everyone. We can maybe talk about some of the work we have been doing on data sharing later on, but there is no perfect way to reach exactly the cohort that you want to reach. The judgment that we took was that reaching 20 million households and having an offer that was more expansive across the population, given what we are facing, was the right thing to do.

At the same time, alongside that, we have more targeted support in the form of the warm home discount, the winter fuel allowance and cold weather payments. This mix of—I will not call it universal, because it is not—near-universal support alongside some level of targeted support provides the right balance. If we had different systems in place and were able to do more targeting based on household income, that would be preferable. We can maybe get into why that is not possible in a moment.

Chair: You mentioned data sharing. What would you like to say about it? Again, it was something that was requested earlier.

Martin McCluskey: I will bring Ben in on this in a moment because he has also been deep in this. In the previous brief that I had as Minister for Energy Consumers, we spent a lot of time earlier this year trying to work out how Government could be more effective at targeting support for households. This is something that has dogged Governments of all types over the years. If we had an accurate record of household income, we would be able to easily target support to people. Unfortunately, we do not.

There are a couple of pieces of work going on that are still happening across Government at the moment. One is a kickstarter programme through DCMS that is looking at how we can build up that database of household income based on existing datasets. I will invite Ben to say a little more about that in a second. That took us part of the way to being able to identify a cohort that we would be able to target, but it was not good enough to rely on for this winter. That is something we are continuing to look at.

The other thing that I would look at in the future and am continuing to look at now is what more we can do with smart meters. We now have a piece of critical national infrastructure in smart metering that has extended to over 70% of the population. There is a question that I always have when I am looking at that programme. Yes, it is now providing reliable metering data to produce reliable bills and everything else you would expect, but are we getting the most out of what has been a significant investment in creating that infrastructure? The answer to that right now is no. It is something that I am continuing to dig into within the Department. Even if we cannot get to that household income level, can we do something more effective with smart metering?

I will invite Ben to say a little bit about the kickstarter and the work we have been doing there.

Ben Golding: I will say a bit about the challenge that the kickstarter is trying to address. The difficulty has always been that in lots of schemes, such as the warm home discount and the household energy payment this winter, we are effectively doing a proxy for low income and vulnerability. Household income would be the best thing we could use to get closest to vulnerable households.

The reason why it is difficult is that often the Government collectively—through HMRC, for instance—hold a lot of data about people’s income because of their tax, but we do not hold that data for people who are self-employed. We do not necessarily hold that data for all households in the same way. It is often very difficult to move from individual income to household income because HMRC will not necessarily know, for instance, who lives in a particular household. It does not always need to have that information in order to tax people. The Government generally hold only the data they require for something.

The kickstarter is trying to look not just at HMRC’s data, but at data held across a whole range of different parts of Government—everything from the Valuation Office to DESNZ to DWP to lots of other places—bring those sources together and explore how we can use quite an innovative set of approaches to work out who is in a household, what the overall income at that household is, and then match that in turn to things such as energy bill meter references. That would give us a much better thing.

It is a remarkably complicated thing to do. The kickstarter is intended to give this a big push. As the Minister said, we would have loved to be able to use that this winter. It is not ready yet, but over the next year or two we will see huge progress in that. It is already coming together. It is the best thing we have, but we are looking at a range of other options alongside that. We are constantly looking at data sources.

Chair: That is helpful. This is hopefully the last question from me; I have massively abused my position as Chair, as my colleagues have pointed out to me. We heard about the impact of removing the gas standing charge and identifying the challenges for some families with children and people with disabilities in particular, but not exclusively. Is there additional support in place for them, because they will see their bills rise on the system that has been outlined?

Martin McCluskey: Let me say something on that briefly and then I might invite Ben to say more if that is appropriate.

Long before the announcement was made on gas standing charges, we recognised that, as soon as you move to more emphasis on the unit rate, there are potential impacts, as you say, Bill, around those people with health conditions or even, in some cases, older people who have to use more heating just to keep themselves warm and healthy. We are going to look in detail at that and at what might be required as part of the work that we are doing on the removal of the gas standing charge. Nobody wants to see unintended consequences from this change that would leave, for example, disabled people or those who rely on medical devices having to pay significantly more. The policy intent is to make things fairer for people; it is not to make energy more expensive.

The Department’s analysis around the time of the Budget said that, without any mitigation, 60% of people would be better off, but, within the population of those who may be worse off, we need to look to make sure that those who are in those categories—for example, disabled people or those with health conditions—are not adversely affected.

Ben Golding: I will add a couple of things. The first is simply to recognise that one of the things that customers feel most frustrated about and that we get the most complaints about is the impact of the standing charge and the lack of control people feel.

The other is that, as well as 60% of people overall benefiting, those benefits are concentrated most at the bottom of the income scale. Overall, this is a progressive measure, but the Minister is completely right: there will be people who would lose out, for reasons outside of their control. Therefore, we are looking at what is the right mitigation for those people.

Chair: Does that include reallocation of the warm home discount?

Ben Golding: There are lots of options on the table. We have not got to exactly what the right way of doing this is yet.

Chair: I have lots more questions, but I had better move on.

Claire Young: Minister, I would like to talk about the plan for warm homes, which has launched after a year-long delay. What is your assessment of the Government’s performance in delivering warm homes since the election, and do you accept that it has been slow?

Martin McCluskey: Maybe the best place to start is to set out the approach that we are taking with the warm homes plan. The first thing to say is that, even before the warm homes plan was published at the start of this year, upgrades were happening. Money was going out through schemes. Local government schemes that we fund were supplying retrofit and home upgrades across the country.

Maybe there has been an impression sometimes given in the political debate that there was a bit of inertia in that period. That is not the case. We had tens of thousands of upgrades happening over that period through local government schemes but also, to go back to the earlier question, through ECO at that point as well.

The warm homes plan really takes us a step ahead and a step up in terms of what we are trying to do on home upgrades across the country. Our target of 5 million homes remains even after the Budget, and that is what we are aiming for, but this is not just about schemes providing people with the support for retrofit; it is also about regulation. Some of the heaviest lifting to get us to those 5 million home upgrades is not through the Government schemes, but through the changes in the future homes standard and through the minimum energy efficiency standards in both the private rented sector and the social rented sector. That is why I can sit here and be quite confident. It is a stretching target, but we are quite confident that we can get to those 5 million homes by 2030 that we promised in the warm homes plan.

I would not want to leave anyone with the impression that, in the period between July 2024 and January 2026, work was not happening. There were a lot of home upgrades happening across the country, so I would not accept the characterisation of it as slow. A significant number of things have happened and are happening now. More will be taking place in the next couple of years, especially as the future homes standard comes into place.

Claire Young: If things were happening, why was the plan so delayed?

Martin McCluskey: The plan sets out a change in the strategic direction of what we are supplying through upgrades. It is not unfair to say that under the previous Government the system was quite reliant on ECO. It was quite reliant on Government support purely for home upgrades. We are moving to a system that is about changing the way that regulation works.

That required a significant amount of work, not just within my Department but across Government. MHCLG, for example, holds responsibility for the building regulations and a lot of the other areas that we were looking to change. That was a complex piece of cross-Government work to get us to where we wanted to be on regulation. We were taking a different approach that demanded us taking time to make sure that we got that right, but, as I said, that was in parallel to a lot of work that was already taking place across the country.

Claire Young: I asked the first panel about the action on fuel poverty and whether they thought there was a long-term strategy or whether it was just about sticking plasters each winter. They were very much in the latter camp. What is your position on that? Do you agree that that has been the position historically? I am sure you are going to want to argue that your approach is different, but how?

Martin McCluskey: It would not be a good use of any of your time if I was to sit and just start criticising the last Government, so I will focus on what we are responsible for and what we have done. We set out the warm homes plan and the fuel poverty strategy this year. Both of those are ambitious, long-term and set out a clear direction—in the case of the fuel poverty strategy, for England—over the coming years.

I can understand why people might look and say that there has been a sticking-plaster approach because we have been in a position of crisis. Being completely blunt about it, we have been in a position of crisis since the invasion of Ukraine by Russia in 2022, which has demanded that each winter we look at what support we have to provide people to meet the requirements of higher energy prices because of rising wholesale prices.

The long-term strategy of this Government is not just to be found in the fuel poverty strategy or the warm homes plan; it is to be found in our drive towards clean power. Ultimately, the thing that is keeping energy bills high and exposing people to these significant peaks and spikes in prices is our exposure to volatile fossil fuels.

In terms of the long-term direction to alleviate fuel poverty and the issue with energy crises in this country, from July 2024 under the previous Secretary of State, we were absolutely clear about where we were going and why we were doing it, which was both for decarbonisation, but also to have more control over our power and more control over the price.

Ultimately, the way that we alleviate fuel poverty is by not being as exposed to gas as we currently are. If the impression has been given that supplying cash each winter makes it look like short-termism, it is not. It is a response to a particular set of circumstances that this country has been facing. If you want to see the long-term direction, look at the clean power plan, the fuel poverty strategy that we launched, and the warm homes plan, because that sets out a very clear and long-term direction for the country.

Claire Young: It is not just about exposure to gas. Many of my residents are on heating oil, for example, and £1 billion has been taken out of the Budget, not for heating but for warm homes in general. How does that fit with having a long-term strategy of moving everyone away from fossil fuels in general?

Martin McCluskey: I will invite David in in a moment, but we faced a significant challenge in order to meet our requirements to defend the country through the defence investment plan. Because of that, we have had to reprioritise budgets. None of us in the Department is going to shy away from the difficult decisions that we had to make.

Despite those reductions in budgets for the warm homes plan, I am confident that we can still deliver what we set out in it, because of the mixture. We are not relying just on Government funding. It is a mixture of Government funding, regulation and also, through things such as the warm homes fund, leveraging more private finance into the system in order to enable people to do that.

I would point as an example to the warm homes loan scheme that we launched two weeks ago, which is already seeing really significant demand. This is a test and learn process, so it has not been accounted for within that 5 million, but it is already showing significant numbers of people taking up solar panels, batteries and heat pumps. Despite the reductions in budget, we can still be ambitious and meet those targets.

Specifically on heating oil, I used to work in and around Scottish politics 10 or 15 years ago, and I spent a lot of time at that point trying to draw attention to the issue of heating oil, because of the number of communities in Scotland that it affects. We went from basically no attention on heating oil 10 years ago, to the Prime Minister at the time standing up at a major press conference and making commitments to heating oil customers as one of the leading parts of his response to the energy crisis in March.

It is not just the £50 million-odd that was put into the crisis and resilience fund for heating oil support, but also that commitment to the CMA investigation, which has now reported and which we have committed to taking forward. That is a really big step forward from where we were on heating oil. I accept that heating oil customers will still face high costs this winter, but we have also offered support, for example, through the boiler upgrade scheme and the £1,500 uplift for those on heating oil, which has seen the number of applications for the boiler upgrade scheme go to its highest ever level. There are a lot of lessons for us to learn from that.

Is there going to be more that we can do in this territory? Of course, but do I think that we have taken a real step forward, especially when it comes to heating oil customers? Yes.

David Thomas: If you stand back slightly, over a decade ago, only roughly a quarter of properties in England were in categories A to C. It is now over half. In the worst-performing categories, there were around a quarter, and now it is less than 10%. This goes back to the point that the Minister was making about regulation.

You cannot change the whole building stock overnight, but if you look over time, you can very much see progress in improving the fabric of homes, which brings bills down. Indeed, Ofgem’s calculations are that the price cap would be about £200 higher if it were not for the fact that consumption over the period has been falling.

As the Minister has said, we have made progress, but there is more to come, which is why we have introduced the private rented sector regulations and the social rented sector regulations through the Energy Independence Bill, which is now in Parliament. The social rented sector has made huge progress, and over three-quarters of homes are now in categories A to C, which is a huge step forward. We need to see similar progress in the private rented sector, and again, by 2030, that will have to have happened. It is another market for the work to be done.

So yes, we are providing support in the meantime, but if you stand back slightly and look at the progress on housing stock, there has been significant improvement over time.

Wera Hobhouse: To follow up on housing stock, many fuel-poor households in Bath live in grade II listed buildings, because we have a lot of them. The change from standing charges to higher unit costs does not help them at all. They are partly heating the sky and still have to turn up the heating, because of simple things such as not even being allowed to replace single glazing with double glazing. Minister, do you have any views about these crazy planning restrictions that are still in place?

Martin McCluskey: I will be really candid about this. We need to go further on what we are doing for rural homes in general.

Wera Hobhouse: This is about urban homes in Bath and planning. People living in grade II listed buildings are not allowed to change their windows from single glazing to double glazing; they are heating the sky.

Martin McCluskey: Sorry, I did not hear your question. We need to make it as easy as possible for people to retrofit their homes. If you take, for example, what we have done around permitted development rights on heat pumps, we have made some really simple changes that have enabled more people to take advantage of the technology. Where there are those restrictions and those regulatory barriers, we need to examine them closely to see whether we can do anything to liberalise them in order to make sure that people are able to take the action that Government are asking them to take.

Wera Hobhouse: This is about listed buildings. Historic England is also taking a view now that buildings are best protected if they are loved and lived in, and yet we still have very restrictive planning conditions in authorities such as Bath, where single glazing cannot be replaced.

Martin McCluskey: I am happy to take those questions away, but, as I said, I am very open-minded—and I hope that people hear what I am saying here—about looking at regulations where it will make it easier for people to upgrade and retrofit their homes. Our objective is that people can live in warm, safe homes that are free of damp. In many cases, the homes that you are probably describing in Bath are not warm and damp-free, so we need to look at how we can improve that.

The Department has done some work already with Historic England and some of the other historic environment bodies across the UK to look at what more we could do. As a Government, we need to look at this closely in order to make sure that people can take that action.

Melanie Onn: Does the definition of fuel poverty meet current expectations of what we would generally understand to be fuel poverty?

Martin McCluskey: At the moment we have the low income low energy—

Melanie Onn: Maybe you could define fuel poverty for the record as well.

Martin McCluskey: Within the LILEE definition that we use at the moment?

Melanie Onn: Yes.

Martin McCluskey: You need to be living in a property that is band D or below and have a disposable income below the poverty line. That is the LILEE definition of fuel poverty.

Melanie Onn: What is the poverty line?

Martin McCluskey: The poverty line at the moment?

Melanie Onn: Yes. What is it in terms of income?

Martin McCluskey: I could not give you that as I am sat here right now, but I would be happy to come back to you on that.

Melanie Onn: It is £212 per week if you are a single individual, £365 if you are a couple, £285 if you are a lone parent, and £519 if you are a couple with two children. It is very low.

Martin McCluskey: Yes, it is very low. In answer to your first question—whether I think it is an adequate definition—we have already committed that we are going to look, through this Parliament, at potentially setting up a new definition of fuel poverty. The way that I would certainly look at it is, “Does the definition that we have at the moment really provide people with a measure of their lived experience?”

When I had my previous brief as Minister for Energy Consumers and we published the fuel poverty strategy, I was very keen that we did not have just the LILEE measure within the fuel poverty strategy, but also an affordability measure. It was important that we published the affordability measure, and we will be publishing that regularly as part of our fuel poverty updates so that we can see a different way of looking at fuel poverty. The affordability measure provides us with a different way of looking at it, which might be more appropriate.

Melanie Onn: For how long are we going to keep just giving people money to try to keep themselves warm through cold periods? We can keep doing that, but Government do not have enough money. They are digging around the back of the sofa to try to fund these things to a very low level that is not meeting people’s needs at all.

That does not solve the issue, and yet we are told in your evidence that taking stock of the retrofitting and the new scheme is going to take us probably beyond 2028, because, if we are thinking about devolution as well, we might have some concerns about how local government or mayors are going to deliver that. We have not really figured out who is going to oversee the scheme. Ofgem did it. The rules were not quite right. We do not know whether we are going to use it again to do any kind of oversight. We have problems with TrustMark. We have an ombudsman that is not meeting the expectations of consumers. People are going to be cold and increasingly experiencing ill health as a result of that until 2029 at the earliest.

Martin McCluskey: Let me take that apart, because there is a lot in that. Let us go back to the first part about whether I think that the definition that we have at the moment is good enough. I do not think that we have really got to the bottom of that.

Melanie Onn: You have said that you are thinking about possibly maybe reviewing it as part of a—

Martin McCluskey: Let me be really clear. The reason why we put an affordability measure in—

Melanie Onn: That tells me that no is the answer, and then we move to the next bit.

Martin McCluskey: Let me just explain, because it is important that I explain what we are thinking. The affordability measure gives us much more exposure to the lived experience of people who are not able to afford their energy bills. It is important that, as Government, we make that really clear, and that is why it is in the fuel poverty updates.

On the other things that you have mentioned, there is a lot in there in terms of our schemes and everything else, but I would take you back a step. We have been very clear, as a Government, especially since July, that we do not think that the way the energy market works is appropriate, which is why we are setting out for more public control and why the 10-year plan will lay out our direction of travel on this.

The point about income support over the period of crisis is really important in order to drive down the cost of energy for people, but the only way that we are really going to drive down the cost of energy is through a combination of the extension of clean power, which I spoke about a moment ago, and those significant market reforms that we are talking about. I am not sitting here and pretending that there are any quick fixes.

Melanie Onn: I appreciate that there is a 10-year plan to get things right going into the future, but what is being provided on the current definition does not meet people’s needs. It does not ensure that they have capacity to warm their homes and keep their children warm through those exceptionally cold periods. If people are old, disabled or suffering with illness, that does not meet the need.

You said beyond 2028. I suggested 2029. You talk about a 10-year plan. It does not give people a sense of hope that there is any urgency in trying to rectify what have been poor schemes that would properly support improved housing in a reasonable timeframe, so that people will be able to experience that before their children have grown up and got a place of their own. How long do people have to wait for?

Martin McCluskey: A lot of people are not having to wait at all because they are getting it now. The schemes that the Government are delivering are being delivered to people now. There is a limit to how much we can deliver each year, because of finances, but we are delivering tens of thousands of home upgrades to people right now through local government schemes, the warm homes social housing fund, and the warm homes local grant.

Melanie Onn: Are these to homes that are in poverty?

Martin McCluskey: These are to homes that are in poverty.

Melanie Onn: Under this Government, how many have been completed under the new Government schemes?

Martin McCluskey: I can write to you with the exact number, but, from memory, it is about 111,000 since 2024.

Melanie Onn: How many do you anticipate will have been completed by next year?

Martin McCluskey: The 2030 target is 5 million home upgrades. As I was saying in response to Claire’s question earlier, it is a mixture of the change in regulation and the Government schemes. The biggest impact that we are going to have in bringing properties up to standard and alleviating fuel poverty is through the changes to the private rental sector minimum energy efficiency standards. Those will come into place in 2030, but landlords are starting to make those changes now in order to comply.

Melanie Onn: If we go on the basis of the trajectory over the past two years, that is only 250,000, not 5 million.

Martin McCluskey: That is just on Government schemes.

Melanie Onn: So you are going to lever in other people.

Martin McCluskey: The warm homes social housing fund and warm homes local grant schemes that we run will continue and provide tens of thousands of upgrades over the next couple of years. What I am saying is that the biggest step forward that we are going to have in terms of upgrading people’s homes is through the regulatory changes that we have made, particularly on minimum energy efficiency standards in the private rental sector, where the new regulations require landlords to increase the energy efficiency of their homes.

In response to an earlier question, I said that the heaviest lifting in getting us to those 5 million home upgrades and lifting a million people out of fuel poverty is through the regulatory changes.

Melanie Onn: Unless they exit the market.

Martin McCluskey: I do not think that this is going to send people to exit the market, and our impact assessment did not suggest that that would be the case either. I was talking about this last week with landlords. Significant numbers of landlords are eager to comply. The support that is on offer for households is also on offer to landlords to help them improve the energy efficiency of their properties. For many landlords, it will be an attractive proposition to be able to do this, but that is what is going to really drive forward progress over the next couple of years.

I will also say that if I have given any impression this morning that we are not acting with urgency, I apologise for that, because we are acting with significant urgency around financial support.

Melanie Onn: I will tell you why I say that, and I can give you some clarity. We have had evidence today from Ofgem and the ombudsman, and they have accepted no responsibility for the quality of installation. Ofgem, which has been the port of call for complaints around the ECO4 scheme between retailers and the ECO4 suppliers, said, “All we had to do was make sure that the numbers happened. Roll-out in no way meant that it had to be fit for purpose.” You say that you accept that there have been failures, but you would not go so far as to say that there is a loss of confidence. You say that it is a very different organisation from a few years ago, and yet, from today’s evidence, I did not necessarily think that. I am interested that you continue to think that Ofgem has a sense of taking on more than a very narrow definition of what overseeing a roll-out really meant.

Martin McCluskey: I do not want to leave anyone with the impression, as I have said a few times, that the way the system ran was appropriate or that it worked. It did not. That is why we are changing the system. That is why we ended ECO and acted with urgency to stop the ECO programme.

Chair: This is about Ofgem’s role, though.

Martin McCluskey: Yes, but just to come back, the point was also around whether we have acted with sufficient haste. What I would say to the Committee is that the consumer protection—

Melanie Onn: No, it was not. It was about confidence in Ofgem continuing, and whether that demonstrates that there is a sense of wanting to fix a broken system.

Martin McCluskey: Let me say to the Committee that I will be really happy, when we publish the Government response on the consumer protection system that will set the system for the future, to come back and talk about that in detail. The questions that you have asked are really important, and we have to make sure that there are high levels of confidence in the system, especially when we are, as a Government, asking people to retrofit and to upgrade their homes.

We are trying, through the new system for consumer protection, to deal with some of the problems that you have just identified, Mel, so I am happy to come back and talk to the Committee about the consumer protection landscape that we are designing to try to make sure that the kinds of problems that happened to ECO never happen again.

I am confident in the warm homes local grant and the warm homes social housing fund that are delivering right now, because they have a level of oversight and audit that was not present in the ECO scheme, which is part of the reason why it failed.

Chair: To really home in on the point about Ofgem, it told us earlier that it was responsible for the number of installations under ECO4, and yet it clearly did not have a process in place, or did not act, to make sure that the numbers that it thought were being installed were what was happening. That is what came out of the first two panels. Is that right? That does run into post-review, Minister.

Martin McCluskey: I will invite David to say something about this in a second, but if you are to take anything from this session this morning in terms of what I am saying in relation to ECO and the way that the system ran, it was a terribly designed system that offered up incredibly high levels of failure, which is why we are changing it and why we are going to be setting out in detail how consumer protection will work in future.

As I said in response to Mel, I am more than happy to come back once that is public, and we can have a full discussion about how that system will operate. My intent with that change in how the system runs is that we are able to give people that level of confidence, which I accept people do not have at the moment.

Chair: Yes, and your less than enthusiastic advocacy for Ofgem earlier was noted.

Martin McCluskey: I will invite David to comment.

David Thomas: Just to be clear, as the Minister said, and as I said earlier, with ECO, the roles were not clear enough, and this is one of the main things that we are trying to fix going forward. To be absolutely clear, Ofgem is not central to rolling out the schemes through local authorities and the social housing fund. We have our own way of overseeing those.

On the boiler upgrade scheme, which was covered briefly in the NAO report, I am not saying that everything is perfect there, but we are not having anything like the same degree of problems. It clearly did not work at all under ECO. We finished that scheme. I have confidence that it is working through BUS in a much better way than it did on ECO, and we are not using it for our main schemes at the moment.

Chair: If Ofgem was lacking on this issue, my concern—and I do not suppose that I am the only person following this discussion who has this concern—is where else we should have concerns about Ofgem.

Martin McCluskey: Let me say two things on that. First, we have concluded the Ofgem review, which recognised that there were issues, including cultural issues, inside Ofgem. That is there in black and white in the Ofgem review documents. It is quite open about the issues that the organisation had and the solutions that we are trying to put in to fix them. I do not think that it would be a surprise to anyone to say that we recognised that there were issues inside Ofgem. That is why we had the review.

We were also ensuring that, post the review, Ofgem now takes on a far more strategic role that is more focused on its regulatory responsibilities and not the slightly sprawling organisation that it has become. That was another conclusion of the Ofgem review. I do not think that it should come as a surprise to anyone that we want to change Ofgem, because we had the review and those were the conclusions from it.

Chair: Should we be concerned that the head of Ofgem, as was, is now the senior official in the Department?

Martin McCluskey: No, we should not be concerned.

Chair: You have to say that, though.

Wera Hobhouse: I have a very quick question about the ombudsman, which also took a hands-off view on ECO and compliance. It said that it sat between consumers and retailers, or the industry, but should the ombudsman not ultimately take a more proactive view on what is good behaviour and promote that, rather than just sitting there neutrally when so much has gone wrong?

Martin McCluskey: The ombudsman has a very specific role within the system as it stands at the moment. In the future system that we are designing—again, I am more than happy to come back once we have published that and go through it in detail—we have been looking at whether there needs to be a statutory ombudsman within the consumer protection landscape in order to make sure that there is proper redress for consumers.

As you will have heard from your witnesses earlier today, and as I have acknowledged all the way through this session when we have been talking about ECO, the system as it exists at the moment sends people from pillar to post. There is no handholding. There is no support on offer. That is what we are trying to fix.

I hope that, when we publish the Government response on consumer protection, a lot of the points that were raised here today are addressed. As I keep saying, I really am more than happy to come back and talk to you about the detail of the consumer protection proposals.

Chair: Can victims of ECO4 seek redress from the ombudsman?

Martin McCluskey: No, not from the ombudsman, but if they are in the find and fix population, they can seek redress through find and fix. Ultimately, the solution to ensure redress for those people who have been affected by this is for the system to deliver redress to them. As I said, we have the voluntary redress fund now, which is new, to deal with those complex cases where they have run out of road and other avenues. I am very conscious that the system is too complicated, which is why we have a proper system for complex cases, so that people are guided and supported through that.

Chair: This session is supposed to be about this winter. We have talked about a lot of things that are wider than this winter. What actions are you and other organisations taking, and what actions can people take, to help today, tomorrow, next week and next month, as the price cap goes up?

Martin McCluskey: We have already taken action in terms of the financial support on offer. I accept that that will—

Chair: In addition to the ones that you have already mentioned. You went through them.

Martin McCluskey: Yes, but it is really important to emphasise that there is significant financial support on offer, especially to the most vulnerable households. Like in any winter, we have prepared, alongside NESO and National Gas, in order to make sure that we have robust security of supply, which we have full confidence in for this winter.

There are a couple of ways to look at that question. If we are talking about the social side and the support that is on offer to people, or if you want to go broader in terms of security of supply and how we are preparing our networks for winter, those are slightly different questions. On the social support side, as I said, we have provided significant—

Chair: Let us focus on the cost of living, because that is probably the one that is foremost in people’s minds.

Martin McCluskey: As I said, we have the significant amount of financial support on offer, and the extended warm home discount. We are rolling out the warm homes plan across the country. We will have schemes delivering solar, batteries and heat pumps across the country this winter.

Chair: That is not going to be delivered to many people this winter.

Martin McCluskey: No, but it is important. We have the extension of the regulation, as we talked about earlier. We also have significant funding through the crisis and resilience fund to local authorities for those people who find themselves in significant levels of distress over this winter period, to make sure that there is financial support additional to the pots of money that I have already spoken about.

Chair: We talked earlier about tariffs, and the mismatch between people on Economy 7 and people getting the right tariffs if they are using storage heaters, for example.

Martin McCluskey: As you would expect, we keep everything under review as we see the forecasts that are coming in terms of the price cap. There is a wide range of tariffs available on the market, and we would always encourage people to look at the tariffs that are most suitable for their individual circumstances. As we install more batteries, solar panels and heat pumps, especially on social housing, for example, that expands the range of tariffs that people are able to access and of support that people are able to receive.

There is a lot in the short term in terms of cash support, in the medium term in terms of what our schemes are providing, and in the longer term in terms of what we are looking at on market reform, which will help people not just this winter but over the coming years.

Chair: You have had 24 hours to reflect on the question that I asked you yesterday about—

Martin McCluskey: York University?

Chair: Indeed, and the very simple take-up of low-cost appliances and the savings available there. Is that the sort of practical advice that you would give?
